p. 25(1) Śrīḥ. Oṃ. Salutations to Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Śiva.
May the flow of ichor streaming from the pair of temples of the elephant-faced one constantly wash away the mass of mud that is the multitude of obstacles. (1.1)
May there be auspiciousness at the beginning, auspiciousness in the middle, and auspiciousness at the end always;
may there be auspiciousness for all the devotees of Śiva and their followers.
Nandikeśvara, who was seated upon the summit of Mount Meru, surrounded by hosts of sages,
the benefactor of the worlds, peaceful, and omniscient.
Rising from among them, the sage Sanatkumāra, the best of Brahmā’s sons and one of great asceticism, questioned him according to the prescribed rite.
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, devoted to the auspicious dharma!
All these people have assembled here, desiring to hear the supreme dharma.
Sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others involve rituals requiring vast wealth;
since they cannot be performed by twice-born men and others who possess little wealth.
Therefore, for the benefit of all mortals, speak of the eternal Śiva-dharma, which is an easy means and accomplishes the purpose of all desires. 1-7.
By which the gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, sages, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, as well as Kiṃpuruṣas and others, were perfected.
And various other groups, devoted to the dharma of Śiva—
all those followers of Śiva’s dharma along with the gods— should be honored with devotion to him. (1.9)
Śrī Nandikeśvara said:
Listen, for I shall declare the supreme Dharma of Śiva, which is the essence of Śiva and the highest among all dharmas— an easy means to attain great fruit.
This was previously told by Śiva to Pārvatī and Ṣaṇmukha,
as well as to the Gaṇas, the chief gods, and especially to us.
For all living beings submerged in the ocean of ignorance,
this glorious Śivadharmottara has been proclaimed as a boat for the sake of their deliverance.
Those who, with tranquil minds, devoted to Śiva and seeking Śiva, practice this supreme dharma—they are Rudras; of this there is no doubt. (1.13)
Whether in a village or in a forest, whether in water or even on dry land—
wherever a *liṅga* is seen, there indeed are all sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Those who remember Virūpākṣa once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or even constantly, should be known as lords of the Gaṇas.
Those men who glorify Rudra even once are swiftly liberated from all sins, even those committed throughout seven lifetimes. (1.16)
Those who always have faith in Rudra are not ordinary human beings;
having attained this world from the realm of Rudra, they are indeed Rudras—of this there is no doubt.
Since the Blessed One was not disregarded by that self-harming person who was born [in this world],
he wanders for a very long time in this saṃsāra, an ocean of suffering. (1-18)
For him, there is a great void—a blindness and muteness of delusion—in that moment or even that hour when he does not contemplate Śarva alone. (1.19)

Having attained this human birth which is so difficult to find, those who worship Sadāśiva have indeed made their birth fruitful; they are the best among men, having accomplished their life's purpose.
But for those who are intent on devotion to Bhava, whose minds are bowed to Bhava, and who are joined with the constant remembrance of Bhava, they are therefore not vessels of suffering. (1.21)
Pleasant dwellings, captivating women adorned with ornaments, and wealth whose end is unseen—these are the fruits of the rite of Śiva-worship. (1.22)
Those who desire great enjoyments, or sovereignty, or even the abode of the thirty gods,
always worship the lotus feet of Hara.
Good fortune, a radiant form, truthfulness, generosity, eloquence, heroism, and world-wide fame—these are the fruits for those who worship Śiva. (1.24)
Those who constantly meditate upon Śiva as the inner controller (antaryāmin) within themselves, for them there always arise the perfections of long life and health. (1.25)
For those who constantly recite [mantras], meditate, always worship Śiva,
and bow down, there is the fruit of the four aims of life and the fourfold liberation.
One who is not Rudra should not remember Rudra; one who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra;
one who is not Rudra should not glorify Rudra; and one who is not Rudra shall not attain Rudra.
Whether through association, curiosity, gain, or even fear, one who should remember,
proclaim, or worship [him] will also inevitably become a Gaṇa. (1.28)
This is the essence of the Śiva-dharma: unwavering devotion to Śiva.
That devotion has been declared by Śiva to have eight limbs; it should be practiced constantly with great effort. (1.29)
The Blessed Lord said: Affection for those who are my devotees, rejoicing in their worship, personally worshipping with devotion, and performing physical activities for my sake; 1.30.
Devotion manifested through changes in voice, eyes, and limbs upon hearing my stories;
constant remembrance of me; and subsisting by means of my glorification—[these are the signs]. (1.31)
This eightfold devotion, even if it exists in an outcaste, makes him a lord of brahmins, a venerable sage, self-controlled, and a wise scholar. (1.32)
Those who, though devoid of wealth, always worship with devotion even with leaves,
flowers, fruits, and water, come to my abode as those equal to me.
Whether it be the implements of worship, or even the very materials for worship, or whatever service has been rendered to me through the actions of mind, speech, and body—[I accept all this]. (1.34)
Even the gift of wealth, gold, or land to him constitutes his worship;
I declare this as the truth: the merit is equal to that of my own worship.
Neither one who has mastered the four Vedas nor even a dog-cooker (outcaste) is dear to me; rather, my devotee is dear.
To him gifts should be given, from him they should be accepted, and he should be honored just as I am.
Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering of the self-disciplined person I accept with a spirit of love. (1.37)
He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me—
for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me. (1.38)
He who, being established in what consists of flesh, does not always worship Me residing within the self, does not find the way through difficult paths even though he is searching for it. (1.39)
He who would see me as all-pervading and everything as established in me—for him I am eternally established in his self, and he is eternally established in me. (1.40)
O Śivā, devotion to Śiva is very difficult to attain; the worship of Śiva is difficult to attain;
the knowledge of Śiva is very difficult to attain; and the fire-oblation to Śiva is difficult to attain. (1.41)
The knowledge of Śiva is very difficult to attain, and its practice is likewise difficult;
yet it should be known that the recitation and meditation whose essence is Śiva are even more difficult to attain. (1.42)
The attainment of these two is extremely difficult; even their practice is hard to find.
Knowing Śiva to be most difficult to attain, one should take refuge in devotion to Śiva. (1.43)
Blessed are those people who have gone for refuge to Śiva;
their mindfulness is constantly fixed upon Śiva, both by day and by night. (1.44)
He on whose tip of the tongue the three syllables "Śivāya," preceded by the salutation and so forth, reside—his life is fruitful. (1.45)
Thus, this entire Śivadharma has been set forth in due order by the month in the first chapter; the remainder is its detailed expansion.
Whoever constantly recites this, or even listens to it with devotion,
is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 1.47 ||
The ḍākinīs of various forms, the rākṣasas, and the leaders of the pretas do not harm him at his sacred seat (pīṭha), nor indeed do any other violent beings.
His enemies shall meet their destruction, he shall attain victory in battle, he shall not be afflicted by any diseases, and calamities shall not touch him. (1.49)
Wealth, long life, fame, knowledge, and incomparable power shall be attained;
through Śumbha, one's desires are constantly fulfilled and reach their fullness. (1.50)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of a Devotee of Śiva," in the glorious Śivadharmottara, proclaimed by the glorious Nandikeśvara.
p. 7 (33) Śrīḥ.
Now begins the second chapter.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Blessed One, O Nandikeśvara, through your special grace, I wish to hear in truth the meritorious procedure for the worship of the Liṅga."
Whatever merit is gained when a *liṅga* is installed, and whatever is gained when a temple of Śiva is built;
whatever merit is gained from sweeping [the shrine], and whatever merit is gained from anointing it with unguents.

Whatever merit arises from the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), from medicinal herbs and seeds, from auspicious bathing and instrumental music, that same merit is obtained by the offering of *arghya* and by the ritual bath with water.
After the application of unguents and before bathing, one should use water mixed with *kuśa* grass and flowers. || 2-4 ||

Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and bathing with curd, whatever merit comes from anointing with ghee, and whatever results from bathing with ghee; || 2-5 ||
Whatever fruit results from [offering] gold, jewels, and water due to their clarity, and whatever may arise from anointing with ointments, perfumes, and the like; || 2-6 ||
By the offering of *bilva* leaves and clusters, by the showing of lamps and mirrors, by worship with loose flowers, and by filling the *liṅga* with garlands; || 2.7 ||
And in the flower-pavilion, by hanging garlands of flowers,
through special acts of worship and devotion, and by the preparation of ointments upon the altar.
Whatever fruit there is in [offering] various species of flowers and also in incenses,
[that same fruit is obtained] by the gift of clothing and ornaments, and by the offering and beholding of lamps. (2.9)
Through the offering of food, edibles, drink, fruits, and roots;
and by means of circumambulation, prostration, salutation, and the recitation of hymns. (2-10)
In the offering of umbrellas, banners, and flags; of bells, musical instruments, and conchs; of canopies, garments, and worship; and in the performance of bali offerings and fire oblations (homa).

Whatever fruit is obtained from the gift of land consisting of elephants, horses, servants, and serpents, and whatever fruit is obtained from the gift of ten villages, market towns, and cities; || 2-12 ||
Whatever merit may accrue to men through the gift of music by women, especially through dance, or by the offering of garlands themselves—[that merit is attained by others]. (2.13)
By the theft of that merit, whatever merit or demerit may arise, as well as the food, drink, and other monastic requisites belonging to ascetics [are likewise lost]. (2.14)
What merit does one obtain by giving [a gift], or by constructing a shelter for them, as well as by performing their consecration, and likewise by rising to meet them and saluting them? (2.15)
Whatever else there may be that has not been prompted by subtle knowledge,
tell all of that to us out of compassion for your devotees.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Distinction of Questions," in the Śivadharmottara.
p. 9 (35) Śrīḥ.
Now begins the third chapter.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O best of the sons of the Lotus-born [Brahmā], you are exceedingly devoted to Śiva;
therefore, I shall tell you everything. Listen with a one-pointed mind. (3-1)
Formerly, when the world had perished in a terrible single ocean and all things mobile and immobile had vanished,
there arose a great dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
"I am the doer, I am the doer; there is no Lord of the world other than me"—thus Brahmā spoke to Hari, and Hari likewise spoke to Brahmā.
To remove the pride of those two gods and to awaken them,
the supreme Taijasa Liṅga of Īśvara manifested between them.
Enveloped in garlands of flames, divine, immeasurable, and incomparable,
it stood ten thousand yojanas wide upon those pure waters.
Deluded by the flames of that *liṅga*, those two best of gods, the lords of the immortals,
were then struck with wonder as they gazed upon it.
Having deliberated with one another regarding his upward and downward movements,
Viṣṇu went below and the Grandfather (Brahmā) went above.
Then, with their palms joined in reverence, they praised the Liṅga;
within the Liṅga stood the Supreme Liṅga, measuring a span.
But those two, established in samādhi and perfected, beheld that which is of the nature of Śiva;
it was neither gold, nor silver, nor copper, nor crystal, nor pearl. (3-9)
That which remains as the mere object of perception is peaceful and absolute, having Śiva as its essence;
Mahādeva, being pleased with those two, granted them an excellent boon.
Having granted him the status of being the cause, he vanished right there;
and from that time forward, the gods and asuras, beginning with Brahmā, established [him].
Likewise, the sages praised the Liṅga as an imitation of that [primordial] Liṅga;
it is the supreme, hidden body, the Liṅga, the beginningless sacred field.
That primordial splendor of the Lord is the Liṅga known by five names;
it is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), manifest and unmanifest, and eternal.
All beings dissolve into it and proceed to the supreme state;
therefore, it is called the *liṅga*, the primordial cause of the worlds. (3.14)
At the end of the kalpa, all the deities dissolve into that liṅga;
Brahmā dissolves into its right side, and Janārdana into its left.
And in the heart is the Gāyatrī, the most excellent among all the gods;
indeed, the Vedas, together with their six ancillaries and the Pada and Krama recitations, dissolve into the crown of the head.
Within his belly, the entire world—both stationary and moving—is dissolved;
from him, it is born again, beginning with Brahmā, including all that is mobile and immobile. (3.17)
They say that space is the *liṅga* and the earth is its pedestal;
it is called the *liṅga* because it is the abode of all beings and because [all things] dissolve into it. (3.18)
Therefore, by installing a *liṅga* that arises from all the gods, everything becomes established and worshipped by him; of this there is no doubt. (3-19)
With palms joined in reverence, Viṣṇu and especially Brahmā first worshipped the Liṅga and then performed their respective duties.
Brahmā always worships the Liṅga with divine, imperishable Vedic syllables;
Brahmā constantly worships the auspicious Liṅga which consists of Śiva.
It is solely through the complete worship of that [Liṅga] that the supreme state of Brahmahood was attained.
Even Śakra, the king of the gods, worships him constantly with devotion; by that [act], he attained the status of Śakra. || 3.23 ||
The giver of wealth (Dhanada) always worships a beautiful linga made of gold;
by that, the god Dhanada attained his status as the giver of wealth.
By means of his supreme state, Vāyu rendered the auspicious [image] born of bile [pure];
through worship at the three times of day, Vāyu did not even attain the nature of wind.
Viṣṇu always worships a linga made of sapphire;
by means of that, he attained the one, eternal, and marvelous Viṣṇu.
The Vasus worship a linga made of bell-metal according to the prescribed rites;
by that, those great-souled ones attained the status of Vasus and great prosperity.
The two Aśvins, worshipping the earthly linga according to the prescribed rites, both attained divine bodies as a result; thus they became the gods known as the Aśvins.
Varuṇa always worships a stainless crystal liṅga;
by that means, he indeed attained the state of Vāruṇa, endowed with supernatural power and strength. (3-29)
The meritorious Liṅga, consisting of food, being meditated upon, offers sacrifice as Agni;
by that act, it has attained the state of Agni, endowed with the form of splendor.
With devotion, the god Divākara worships a liṅga made of śaiva-tāmra three times a day; by that act, he attained the supreme state of Sūrya.
Soma always worships a linga made of pearls;
by that act, Soma attained his eternal and radiant state as the Moon.
The best of serpents worship a linga made of coral;
by that means, they have attained among the Nāgas a supreme state rich in enjoyments. (3.38)
By means of the fragrance of the worshipful one, the Gandharvas attained their state as Gandharvas;
likewise by means of fruit, cow dung, wood, and flowers. (3.34)
Through their intention and through the essence alone, many shall attain their desired goal;
the best of the Asuras worship a linga made of black iron.
Those high-souled Rākṣasas, whose prowess was sharpened by him,
were Piśācas who worshipped a linga made of tin and lead.
Supported by the power of great supernatural faculties (mahardhi), they attain the supreme state; the Mothers always worship a linga made largely of iron.
Having attained motherhood, all of them proceed to the supreme state;
even so do the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
They worship Īśāna, the leader of the gods, at all times. (p.
13) The entire world consists of the *liṅga*; everything is established within the *liṅga*. 3-39.
Therefore, one should worship the *liṅga* if one desires success for oneself;
for in the *liṅga*, the Great God, Mahādeva, is himself directly established.
Therefore, for the sake of favoring the worlds, one should worship the Liṅga;
he who, out of delusion, does not worship the Liṅga of the Lord of the three worlds [incurs sin]. (3–41)
His birth should be known as futile and his lineage as meaningless;
he is not a fit vessel for heaven, nor for liberation, nor for sovereignty. (3.42)
But he who constantly worships the Liṅga, the Lord of the three worlds, quickly becomes a recipient of heaven, liberation, and sovereignty. (3.43)
Therefore, having become single-minded, the wise man, even when in distress, should always worship Mahādeva for as long as he lives, according to his vow. (3.44)
Having extracted [the lineage] up to the seventh generation, it dissolves together with Śiva.
Better is the renunciation of life, or even the cutting off of one's head. (3-45)
But one should not eat without having first worshipped the three-eyed Lord;
he who thus carries out this vow for as long as he lives— (3.46)
Bound by a human skin, he is Rudra; there is no doubt about this.
There is no merit greater anywhere than the merit derived from the worship of the *liṅga*. (3-47)
Thus having understood this, Sadāśiva should always be worshipped without effort;
there is no other means for men to cross the ocean of worldly existence. (3.48)
The worship of the *liṅga* is a boat for those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
He who hates the *liṅga*, which is saluted by all the gods, [commits a sin]. (3.49) p. 14 (40)
A man would go to hell even by conversing with him;
for Maheśvara has created the entire triple world, including all that is mobile and immobile. (3.50)
Those who do not worship with their intellect the Inner Self of the worlds, by whom Maheśvara is worshipped as the devotee, become ungrateful in this world. (3.51)
He should be known as a traitor to himself and remembered as a traitor to his ancestors, because in all beings resides the divine Maheśvara as their refuge. (3.52)
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in Śiva alone;
for even the oceans may be exhausted, and even the Himavat mountain may waste away.
There is no exhaustion of the world of Rudra for those who have taken refuge in Śaṅkara.
One should desire many sons who follow the mantras of Śiva. (3.54)
They rescue their lineage just as a rope rescues a jar from a well; having thus rescued it, they indeed deliver twenty-one generations of their family. (3.55)
They indeed quickly attain the state of Śiva, freed from both merit and demerit.
Two types of liṅgas have been described: the mobile and the immobile. (3.56)
The moving is well-known as that which is perceived [in living beings], while the non-moving is found in things such as the earth;
Maheśvara dwells eternally within the moving, endowed with affection. (3.57)
Through the purification by mantra within the conduct, Sadāśiva is eternally the truth of both;
the two-fold [reality] consisting of the stationary and the moving is thus declared.
Through the disparagement of the mobile, the immobile becomes fruitless;
therefore, a wise and learned person should not despise these two types of liṅgas. (3.59)
Having thus established the *liṅga* with every effort according to the prescribed ritual, listen to the merit [that is gained]... [3.60]
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and visiting sacred fords—
that fruit a man obtains multiplied ten millionfold by installing a liṅga.
Whoever should establish a single linga according to the prescribed rites, accompanied by sacrificial fees—
that meritorious linga proclaimed in all the Agamas shall yield ten million times the merit.
By rescuing the three lineages— those of his mother, his father, and those from whom he takes a wife— he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, when the dissolution [of the world] has arrived,
he establishes himself in the yoga of knowledge and is liberated right there.
If, however, he should desire sovereignty, he will be born in another existence as the lord of the earth consisting of the seven continents and oceans. || 3.65 ||
He who, having fashioned a clay linga, worships it according to the Vedic rites,
becomes wealthy and glorious in this very world, and in the end, he is born as Rudra.
Having fashioned an earthen image, one should worship the Liṅga at the three junctions of the day;
hear now the fruit of his merit until the completion of eleven hundred [offerings].
With this very body, Rudra remains upon the earth, destroying the sins of all mortals through both sight and touch. (3.68)
Having extracted [the deceased] and established them in heaven for twenty-one generations,
he rejoices eternally in the celestial realm together with his companions, like Rudra himself. (3.69)
A linga made of rice-flour paste, adorned with fragrant substances,
and further embellished with sweet-smelling flowers and various kinds of fruits.
A wise man should place agarwood on its right side, together with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, as well as ghee and cakes.
One should place beautiful realgar in the western part;
one should place sandalwood in the north, and yellow orpiment is likewise honored there.
Having thus performed the extensive display of wealth according to one's means,
one should offer it to Śiva on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Whosoever, being wise, should fashion such a linga even once—listen as I declare to you the fruit that he also obtains. (3.74)
Released from evil through hearing [this], and freed from all suffering, one becomes partless and omnipresent, and shall enter the imperishable Śiva. (3.75)
Even by making a linga the size of an āmalaka fruit and worshipping it, one who is absorbed in me and becomes identical with me is glorified in the world of Śiva. (3.76)
Upon the exhaustion of merit, having reached the earth, he becomes a righteous king;
or else he is born as a Brahmin who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. (3.77)
Having fashioned a linga from clay, ashes, a lump of cow dung, or even sand,
and having worshipped it but once, one shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas.
Whoever should draw [the mandala] with the tips of kusha grass, or on a tree, a wall, or even with a finger,
for ten thousand aeons during play, he too shall become a Lord of the Ganas. (3.79)
Whatever is beneficial for oneself as well as for others,
when performed with certainty in every respect together with one's kinsmen, purifies the family unto the seventh generation.
Furthermore, that man who fashions a linga while playing in the dust obtains, after death, a prosperous kingdom free from all thorns. (3.81)
Those who are born among those of low status and those men who are most sinful, as well as those who have taken refuge in Bhava with true devotion, are liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
He who, though not possessing the marks [of an ascetic], lives by means of the mark in the form of a mark, is cooked for an inexhaustible time in a most terrible hell. (3.83)
Even through a subtle application, one obtains immeasurable fruit;
therefore, because Śiva is being worshipped, one should worship him constantly. (3.84)
O beginningless Lord of the gods, Sovereign of the universe, Great Lord;
O omniscient one, sole bestower of knowledge and realization—salutations be unto You! (3.85)
O you who are endowed with infinite splendor, seated upon an infinite throne, enjoying infinite power—O Supreme Lord, homage be to you! 3-86
O Supreme Lord, who transcend the high and the low, the cause of the origin and sustenance [of the world], and the means for accomplishing all goals—homage be to You! (3.87)
O you of many forms, O great form, O supreme among all forms! O you who have transcended the ocean of bonds that fetter the individual soul, may you, the bestower of boons, be victorious!
O Sadāśiva, whose nature is pure and effortless, who pervades all;
O Lord of Yoga, Great Yogi, Master of Yoga—homage be to you! (3.89)
O stainless one, O supportless one, O you who are the support of all and free from agitation;
O gracious Supreme Lord, O Lord of Yoga, homage be to you! (3.90)
Indeed, whatever I have experienced through the fickleness of my tongue, that should be forgiven by you, O incomparable one; for who can praise you, an ocean of virtues? (3.91)
The man who constantly hears this meritorious hymn to the origin of the *liṅga* is not born again in *saṃsāra*, but attains the eternal state. (3.92)
Therefore, one should listen with every effort...
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Origin of the Liṅga," in the glorious Śivadharmottara.
Glorious One! Now begins the fourth chapter.
O Śrī Nandikeśvara, those who are devoted to Śiva, possessed of great enthusiasm, dedicated to the worship of Śiva,
self-restrained, and endowed with all prosperity— they accomplish all their goals. (4.1)
Enduring all dualities with fortitude, always possessing minds of constant exertion, devoted to the welfare of others, and intent upon serving their gurus. (4.2)
They are upright, gentle, clear-sighted, compliant, and pleasant of speech;
they are free from pride, possessed of wisdom, and have abandoned rivalry and desire. (4.3)
They are peaceful, with smiling faces, auspicious, and always welcoming;
they speak little yet are eloquent, and are experts in devotion to their gurus.
Endowed with purity and proper conduct, abiding in compassion and courtesy, they are free from hypocrisy and envy, and speak only what is true and factual.
Devoted to sharing, wise, free from deceit, and beyond reproach, they remain unstained by sense objects, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.

Rivers are not turbid merely because they flow through various impurities; likewise, those who have cultivated their selves do not succumb to the power of passion or anger, for they are exceedingly gentle and devoted to the service of the virtuous.
Those who have abandoned all attachments do not fall under the sway of their feet, hands, speech, eyes, ears, or genitals, nor do they engage in restless movements.
Those men on earth whose conduct is of such a kind as this— having Rudra as their self, being devoted to Rudra, being portions of Rudra, and being permeated by Rudra— [become so]. (4-9)
For one who abides in these qualities by resorting to exclusive devotion,
life itself is always to be honored for the sake of attaining both the supreme and the lower states.
One vessel consists of the Vedas, and another vessel consists of austerity;
whichever vessel arrives shall deliver that [other] vessel.
The Veda is Śiva, and Śiva is the Veda; the student of the Veda is Sadāśiva.
Therefore, those who are devotees of Śiva should give to one who knows the Veda according to their capacity.
O Maheśvaras, Śrī Nandikeśvara is the supreme recipient among all recipients,
for he protects one from falling into the exceedingly deep ocean of hell. (4-13)
By virtue of the greatness of that vessel, even that gift becomes inexhaustible;
therefore, those who desire immeasurable fruit should always give to him.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, recited, or presented as worship and oblation to Śiva, that yields exclusively infinite fruit; of this there is no doubt. (4.15)
Whether one constructs a collection of temples out of devotion or in accordance with one's wealth—be it small or large—the fruit is equal for both the rich and the poor. (4.16)
Even a wealthy man who performs a religious duty with stinginess regarding his wealth does not obtain its fruit, for his mind is overcome by greed. (4.17)
Since life is impermanent, even a person of meager wealth, impelled by devotion, should set aside two portions for the sake of Dharma. (4.18)

Even one who possesses the essence of great wealth would not [attain the goal] if devoid of devotion; for he who, though devoid of devotion to Śiva, might give away even his entire property [would gain nothing]. (4-19)
Therefore, one does not partake of the Dharma by that [means]; rather, devotion alone is the cause in this matter—not by those most fierce austerities, nor by all the great sacrifices.
He who builds a temple for Śiva out of clay, wood, bricks, or stone, having abandoned devotion whose essence is Śiva, shall go to the divine city of Śiva. (4.21)
Accompanied by thirty-seven generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. The merit derived from a temple made of wood is ten million times greater than that of one made of clay.

In a temple of Śiva, the measurement for wooden structures and so forth may exceed by one [unit] up to ten million times ten million; however, for stone temples, it should be double that of brick structures and the like.

The merit of [shrines] made of clay and stone should be known as equal, as well as that of the wealthy and the poor; wherever a meritorious work made of stone or brick is performed with devotion, [therein lies the fruit]. (4.24)
Therefore, whoever constructs a temple of Śiva even without ancient scriptures, having shaken off the multitude of his sins, he too shall go to the abode of Śiva. (4.25)
Even while playing, he who constructs a temple of Śiva during his childhood shall attain the world of Rudra, and a celestial chariot that travels everywhere shall be his.
It was encircled by garlands of flowers, resounded with divine fragrances and celestial music,
equipped with swinging cradles, and adorned with bells and yak-tail fans.
Adorned with a canopy of pearl necklaces, possessing a brilliance equal to the sun, crowded with throngs of celestial nymphs, it bestows all desires and happiness. (4.28)
Having dwelt there in great enjoyments, happy for ten million times ten million ayutas,
he gradually returns to this world and becomes a righteous king. || 4-29 ||
Seeing and avoiding living beings, one should sweep slowly with a soft and fine broom; thus one shall obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (4.30)

One should collect cow dung in the pen from a cow that has not died due to lack of food, one that has recently calved, one whose calf is emaciated, nor from one afflicted by disease, nor from one that does not give birth. (4.31)
One should take cow dung that has settled on the ground or fallen in an auspicious place;
having discarded what is from above or below, it should be fresh and free of insects.
He who performs the smearing [of the floor] with water filtered through a cloth, while observing and avoiding living beings, shall obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (4.33)
He is a sage, he is a great saint, he is a yogi; he shall go to Śiva.
All gifts, sacrifices, fire-offerings, and ritual oblations are subject to decay; however, the great gift of fearlessness toward all embodied beings does not decay.
He who performs sweeping and anointing without interruption for a fortnight is honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred times ten million divine yugas.
And at its conclusion, one becomes a righteous king, a master of the four Vedas, handsome in appearance, wealthy, and endowed with all virtues. (4.37)
Even a man who performs an act in the abode of Śiva merely through association shall, after attaining knowledge beyond the three bodies, reach peace. || 4.38 ||
By rejecting the body of Rudra, one may attain some degree of knowledge; however, only a rare few on earth, having attained such knowledge, are liberated. (4.39)
All embodied beings wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering and grief, as long as they do not become devotees of Śiva. (4.40)
If the mind of a living being were attached to the auspicious (Śiva) in the same way as it is attached to the sphere of sensory objects, who indeed would not be liberated from bondage? (4.40)
Whoever should have the ground paved so that it resembles the surface of a mirror, variegated with various cloths and radiant with diverse flowers; || 4.42 ||
In some places it was arranged with water-jars, adorned with lotuses and the like,
level and even, and situated within the precincts of a temple of Śiva.
For as many thousands of yugas as there would be earth measured all around by the length of the staff, for that long one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Whoever should have a temple of Śiva plastered with lime using every possible effort shall obtain that merit for as long as the temple remains standing.
And the wise man who should build a temple for Śambhu every year, making it white with milk and nectar and beautiful with various pigments; || 4.46 ||
For as many years as one makes that temple of Śiva white,
for that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Rudra.

One should diligently have paintings executed in the temple of Śiva by those learned in the treatises on painting, using subjects such as the sports and incarnations of Rudra as prescribed in the Āgamas.
As many forms of Rudra as one may have depicted here in beautiful form, for that many thousands of aeons one is glorified in the world of Rudra. (4.49)
Whoever repairs what is broken or cracked in a temple of Śiva,
or even restores a garden there, obtains the worldly fruit.
There is no god equal to Rudra; there is no teacher equal to Rudra.
There is no knowledge equal to Rudra; there is no austerity equal to Rudra.

Salutations to you, the Lord of Gods, whose stainless body has been shaken free from impurity, whose form is pure by its very nature, and who is adorned with white ash as an unguent for the limbs. 4-52.
Salutations be to you, the blue-throated one, to Śarva, to the victorious one, to the white-bodied one, to the multiformed, to the beloved, and to the eternal. 4-53.
Salutations to you, the Supreme, the Highest Lord, the Omniscient;
salutations to you, the Lord of the Universe, whose multitude of qualities transcends all.
Salutations to you, the infinite one, who wears a necklace of great lordly serpents, who is beautiful with tawny eyes, and who is enriched by manifold deeds. 4-55.
Salutations be to you, who are yourself unprostrated while all bodies prostrate before you; who are worthy of worship even by those who are themselves worshipful; and who are without a protector.

Salutations to you, who are worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu; who are the cause of the origin and sustenance [of the world]; who bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; and who are ever self-restrained.
Salutations to you, the left-handed one, who possesses a beautiful form, who reveals the conduct of the left-handed path, whose body is half-composed of your beloved Vāmā, and who are infinite.
He who shall recite this meritorious and supreme chapter with faith,
being liberated from all sins, shall attain union with Śiva. (4.59)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Abodes of Śiva," in the Śivadharmottara, a venerable scripture of the Śaiva tradition.
Glorious One. Now begins the fifth chapter.
Śrī Nandikeśvara should perform auspicious rites, such as the utterance of the word "Victory," at the time of bathing Maheśa Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who is embodied as the Liṅga. 5-1.
With [the marks] such as the trident, vajra, conch, lotus, śrīvatsa, and svastika, fashioned upon vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth, using cow dung and other substances. || 5-2 ||
It was filled with unbroken rice grains and sesame seeds of various colors combined together, mixed with white mustard and curd, arranged so as to be beautiful.
With parched grains, flour-lamps and the like, with sprouts of mango, *aśvattha*, and other trees, with pure medicinal herbs, with all kinds of seeds, and with barley sprouts; || 5.4 ||
On all days beginning with the eighth, during festivals,
at all auspicious times, and on the holy full-moon day of the month of Pauṣa.

One should perform an auspicious lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for the *liṅga*, dedicated to Śiva, accompanied by the great sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, along with songs. (5–6)
O Śivā, for as many parvas as one performs the nīrājana rite according to the rules,
for that many thousands of yugas one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who performs singing and instrumental music, or dance, or vocal music, at the time of bathing or during the three junctions of the day. || 5-8 ||
For as many years as one performs singing, dancing, instrumental music, and the like,
for that many thousands of yugas one is glorified in the world of Rudra. (5-9)

One should bathe [the deity] with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water infused with kuśa grass and purified by mantras; indeed, that is remembered as the "Brahma-bath" (brahmasnāna).
He who performs the Brahma-bath at the Linga for even a single day,
having shaken off his sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
A bath with the five products of a tawny cow—curd, milk, and ghee—is known to be a hundred times more effective than any other; of this there is no doubt. (5.12)
Therefore, for the sake of the perpetual fire-sacrifice to the gods and for the purification of the body,
one should take a tawny cow (kapilā), which is honored by sages, gods, and others.
The Śūdra who drinks the milk fit for divine rites, belonging to the followers of Kapila,
is cooked for a very long time in the most terrible ocean of hell.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of years, it all burns away by anointing the Liṅga with ghee; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of eons,
all that is consumed by a bath of ghee, just as fire consumes fuel.

Having performed a bath with ghee on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, a man who does so even once at the Liṅga uplifts twenty-one generations of his lineage and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
A practitioner of yoga who has mastered the Vedas should give ten thousand milch cows, provided with clothing, gold, and other ornaments, after bathing them in ghee; such is the fruit of that act.
The man who bathes the *liṅga* once with a *droṇa* measure of milk is honored in the world of Soma by means of a silver celestial chariot. (5-19)
Just as a man who bathes the liṅga once with curd with true devotion becomes liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. (5.20)
That man who bathes the Liṅga even once with honey out of devotion,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Agni.
One should bathe [the image] with sesame oil produced by a hand-press;
having been anointed with white paste, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
Whoever performs the ritual bath of the Liṅga even once with sugarcane juice shall attain the world of the Vidyādharas, endowed with all objects of desire. || 5.23 ||
The man who, out of devotion, bathes the Liṅga with the water from the fruit,
having cast off the mire of his sins, is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
Having bathed the liṅga once with white ashes, one rejoices;
pure as a moonbeam and glorious, one dwells within the orb of the moon.
He who bathes the Liṅga even once with water filtered through a cloth shall attain a soul fully satisfied in all its desires and reach the world of Varuṇa. || 5-26 ||
Whoever bathes the Liṅga even once with devotion using Kuśa-grass water is honored in the world of Brahmā, traveling in a golden celestial chariot. || 5-27 ||
If one bathes the Lord even once with water scented with sandalwood, one attains the world of the Gandharvas and is honored by the Gandharvas. (5.28)
Having reached the world of Savitṛ with water from flowers, that of Kubera with golden water,
and that of Mahendra with water containing jewels, he rejoices. (5-29)
Pāṭala, utpala, padma, and karavīra flowers— smooth and fragrant— should always be added to the bathing waters.
Whoever performs even one of these ablutions with devotion toward Śiva,
having shaken off the mire of sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.

Whoever bathes the Liṅga even once with camphor and aloe-wood water consecrated by the recitation of the mantra one hundred and eight times; whoever bathes the Liṅga even once with camphor and aloe-wood water— || 5.32 ||
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
[he who worships] Śiva with pure water over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times.
Having bathed [the deity] once with devotion, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
likewise, having bathed the Liṅga once with devotion on the eighth day of the dark fortnight while fasting, [one attains the same].
Having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
he who, intending for his ancestors, bathes the Liṅga with the water of Śiva.
The ancestors, even from hell, shall go to heaven satisfied,
having bathed the Liṅga with cool water as well as with a stream of warm milk.
Having bathed [the deity], the performance of the ghee-bath (ghṛtasnāna) is indeed distinguished;
having performed these three baths and having worshipped with devotion, || 5.37 ||
A person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices;
bathing with a copper vessel from a clay jar yields a hundredfold greater merit.
The merit from [a linga made of] silver is ten thousand times greater than that of gold; the fruit from one of gold is more than ten million times greater.
The sight of the linga is meritorious, and touching it is even more auspicious than seeing it. (5-39)
Worship through touch is superior, and bathing with ghee is even better than that.
By means of a bath of ghee, the sins committed by embodied beings in this world and the next [are destroyed]. (5.40)
Since Śaṅkara casts [the impurity] away, one should therefore perform a ritual bath;
with water one removes ten offenses, and likewise with milk, a hundred.
One may destroy a thousand [sins] with curd, and likewise ten thousand with ghee; one may destroy a hundred thousand with honey, and ten million with sugarcane juice. (5.42)

He who performs the ritual bath of Śiva with coconut leaves for ten million times, with fragrant waters for infinite times, and who continuously performs the ghee-bath for a month— [attains the aforementioned fruit]. (5.43)
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he sports in heaven like Rudra;
bathing is known to yield a hundredfold fruit, while anointing the body yields twenty-fivefold.
A thousand fruits are proclaimed as the great bath (*mahāsnāna*);
one should diligently bathe the Liṅga with oil massage and ghee. (5.45)
Listen to the fruit of his merit from [an offering] made with the flour of barley and wheat:
surrounded by celestial women with yak-tail whisks held in their outstretched hands, he [shall dwell in heaven]. (5.46)
Abiding in a celestial mansion of great enjoyment, one shall go for a long time to the city of Śiva;
by this method of worship, infinite merit [is obtained]. (5.47)
Sanatkumāra, tell me: with how many kinds of flowers should worship be performed?
Nandikeśvara [should worship] with flowers produced from Āraṇḍa or with leaves grown on the mountain.

One should worship Śiva with flowers that have not been stale overnight, which are free from holes, sprinkled with water, devoid of insects, and whether grown in one's own garden or otherwise obtained.
The merit found among various species of flowers would not be greater than that;
therefore, [merit is greater] when given to a worthy recipient (pātra) who is endowed with the virtue of moral conduct and has mastered the Vedas.
The fruit obtained by giving ten pieces of gold when Śiva is worshipped is the same as that for whoever offers even a single arka flower to Śiva. (5.51)
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving ten pieces of gold, one shall obtain even greater fruit than that through this particular flower. (5.52)
Learn now that other flower by which [the rite] becomes effective; listen to how it is:
the *karavīra* is superior to thousands of *arka* flowers. (5.53)
A single *jāti* flower excels a thousand *karavīra* flowers;
a single lotus excels a thousand *jāti* flowers. (5.54)
The *bakapuṣpa* flower excels over a thousand *padma* flowers;
a single *dhurdhūraka* flower is superior to a thousand *bakapuṣpa* flowers. (5.55)
A single *bṛhatpuṣpa* flower is superior to a thousand *dhurdhūraka* flowers;
a single *droṇapuṣpa* flower is superior to a thousand *bṛhatpuṣpa* flowers. (5.56)
Apāmārga is superior to thousands of Droṇa flowers;
Kuśa flower is superior to thousands of Apāmārga flowers. (5.57)
A single *śamī* flower is superior to a thousand *kuśa* flowers;
a magnificent blue lotus is better than a thousand *śamī* flowers. (5.58)
Among all species of flowers, the preeminent is the blue lotus;
yet the bilva leaf is superior to thousands of blue lotuses. (5.59)
There exists no leaf more dear to Śiva than the bilva leaf;
it possesses the very nature of the syllables of the Praṇava, bestows knowledge of the three periods of time,
brings victory over the three worlds, and removes the three kinds of sin.
Those [lotuses] were produced together with nectar and Śrī in the ocean;
by worshipping Śrī with three petals, one attains liberation. || 5.62 ||
A single act of devotion excels thousands of leaves and flowers;
hear now the fruit of the merit of one who worships Śiva with devotion according to the prescribed rule. (5–63)
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas, the illustrious one, possessing prowess equal to Śiva, shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
The fruit of all other species of flowers has been proclaimed;
according to that fruit, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The *śamyā* and the *bṛhatī* are said to be equal to the *kusuma*;
the *dūrvā* is equal to all flowers; one should worship together with *droṇa* and *bilva*.
The Karavīra is known to be equal [in merit], as are the Jātī, Kuṭaja, and Pāṭala;
the white Mandāra flower shall be equal to the white lotus. (5–67)
The *nāga*, *caṃpaka*, *puṃnāga*, and *ghurghuraka* are considered equal [in quality]; as are the *ketakī*, *atimukta*, *kunda*, *yūthī*, and *madantikā*. (5.68)
One should avoid flowers of the śirīṣa, sajjabandhūka, vāgujī, and karañja, as well as leaves from the indrataru tree. (5–69)
One should avoid the leaves and flowers of the *vibhītaka* tree;
one should avoid whatever flowers are scentless or have a pungent odor.
One should not reject fragrant and pure flowers;
even that which is devoid of fragrance is to be accepted if it is pure, such as kuśa grass and the like. (5.71)
Just as there is delight in a scentless flower, so too is there delight for Śiva, who is devoid of qualities;
that flower is sattvic if it is fragrant, and tāmasika if it is impure.
Kadamba groves should be offered to Śaṅkara at night;
flowers that remain from the day [should be offered] during the day, and the mallikā both by day and by night.
The *jāti* flower remains [pure] for a day and night;
Śambhu resides in the *karavīra* for three nights. (5.74)
The *bilva* fruit [should be offered] for three months, half a month, or even ten or three days,
because it is extremely dear to Śiva and Śivā and because it originates from the tree of immortality (*amṛtadruma*).
Because it is free from the fault of being stale, those seeking liberation should employ [such food] for the sake of auspiciousness;
however, [food] infested with hair or insects, or that which is decayed and stale, [should be avoided]. (5.76)
And having himself bathed [the image] with fallen powders and perfumed decoctions, he should subsequently bathe it with pleasantly warm water.
One should sprinkle [the deity] with bilva leaves and likewise purify the pedestal;
one obtains that fruit which is gained by giving ten thousand cows. (5.78)
A mortal obtains that fruit when the anointing of the Liṅga has been performed;
he who offers to Śiva an oblation consisting of water along with flowers and water for the guest-offering (arghya) [attains it]. (5.79)
He is worthy of worship in all worlds and rejoices for a long time like Śiva;
[he should offer] water mixed with scented water as the *arghya* offering, ten times more than the previous amount.
The *arghya* mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) becomes tenfold [in merit].
Having filled the eight-limbed *arghya*, one should offer it upon the top of the *liṅga*. (5.81)
One is glorified in the world of Rudra for ten thousand years by offering water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, curd, clarified butter, and rice. (5.82)
Likewise, eight types of arghya offerings made with sesame seeds and white mustard seeds have been proclaimed;
the fruit that one obtains by offering [these] with a wooden arghya vessel—[that fruit is attained]. (5.83)
By the offering of an arghya with a copper vessel, the merit is a hundred times greater.

An offering made with leaves of the Palāśa or lotus is equal to one made in a copper vessel; it should be known that an offering made in silver is worth more than a hundred thousand times [the former].
The water for respectful offering (arghya) placed in a golden vessel is increased a crore-fold;
thus, one proceeds in order with the bath, arghya, food offerings (naivedya), sacrificial oblations (bali), incense (dhūpa), and so forth.
The fruit of that does not increase further by means of a particular difference in the vessel;
however, the fruit obtained by one who has mastered the Vedas through the gift of a silver vessel [is far greater]. (5.87)
Therefore, the merit from giving an earthen vessel to Śiva is a hundred times greater than that which would accrue to one who has mastered the Vedas from giving a golden vessel. (5.88)

O Śivā, the merit gained from the gift of a copper vessel is a hundred times greater than that; and for one who has mastered the Vedas, the merit of giving ten million pieces of gold is likewise vast.
The merit of one who offers a silver vessel to Śiva is great;
however, the merit of one who, with devotion, presents a golden vessel to Śiva is even greater.
It is impossible to describe the entirety of his merit;
it is declared that the fruit is exactly the same for both the wealthy and the poor through Śiva. (5.91)
Between those two as well, he who has greater devotion toward Śiva is superior;
for even when wealth is available, he who, out of delusion, does not perform the elaborate ritual procedures [is inferior].
One whose mind is overcome by greed does not obtain that fruit at all;
therefore, whatever has been performed with leaves, fruits, water, and so forth— [5.93]
That should be known as having infinite fruit; devotion alone is the cause here.
One should perform the smearing of the Liṅga with divine and fragrant perfumes. (5.94)
One is glorified in the world of Rudra for a hundred divine crores of years;
the merit from anointing with sandalwood paste is twice that of other fragrant unguents.
The merit derived from agallochum (agaru) is known to be eight times greater than that of sandalwood;
specifically, the fruit of black agallochum is held to be double that amount. (5.96)
Therefore, a hundred times more merit is prescribed for saffron than for sandalwood,
agallochum, and camphor when these are finely ground together with saffron.
Having thoroughly anointed the *liṅga*, one shall dwell in heaven for ten million eons (*kalpa*);
likewise, having fanned the *liṅga*—which has been smeared with fragrant unguents—with a palm-leaf fan. (5.98)
Having offered a beautiful palm-leaf fan to Rudra with devotion, one is honored in the world of Vāyu for thousands of millions of years.
Having offered a peacock-feather fan that is exceedingly beautiful to Śiva, one is glorified in the world of Rudra for ten thousand years. (5.100)
One is honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred million years;
one should offer a fly-whisk to Śiva, adorned with a handle and a ring.
Or [he may offer] a staff made of gold, silver, and so forth; hear now the fruit of his merit.
He should cast away the flowers that have been offered during the worship of the Auspicious Śambhu.
One should not worship the deity with unopened buds, nor should one offer uncooked food.
One should carefully discard even ripe fruit that has been pecked by a hawk.
If flowers are not obtained, one should offer even leaves;
and in the absence of leaves, one should offer dūrvā grass, droṇa, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
In the absence of dūrvā grass, droṇa rice, and sesame seeds, one should also offer fruits;
and in the absence of even fruits, one may offer grasses, shrubs, and medicinal herbs.
In the absence of medicinal herbs, he becomes honored through devotion;
for each individual flower offered, the fruit is ten pieces of gold.
In those very same arrangements of garlands, twice the fruit is desired for one who properly worships the Liṅga with fragrant loose flowers. (5.107)
Or by means of fragrant garlands, one shall obtain the fruit of the sound [of the mantra];
one should worship the liṅga even once with unbroken bilva leaves. (5.108)
Freed from all sins, that man who worships the Liṅga even once with gongs (ghurghurakas) is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 5.109 ||
Having obtained the fruit of a hundred thousand cows, he is glorified in the world of Śiva—
he who, with devotion, worships a liṅga even once with bṛhatī flowers.
Having obtained the fruit of the gift of ten thousand cows, one shall go to Śiva;
[one should offer] jasmine, blue lotuses, red lotuses, jasmine, punnāga, and campaka flowers.
Aśoka, śveta-mandāra, karṇikāra, and bakula;
karavīra, arka, mandāra, śamī, tagara, and kesara. (5.112)
With kuśa grass, apāmārga, and flowers produced from kadamba and droṇa trees, as well as with saugandhika, āsana, agastya, sindu, sephālikā, and arjuna flowers.
A garland made from *tulasī*, *kurava*, *kola*, *nāga*, *vañcula*, *nandyāvarta*, *śamyāka*, and *tilaka* [is auspicious]. (5.114)
With other fragrant leaves grown in villages or forests,
or even with flowers as they may be obtained, that man who worships Śiva— (5.115)
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit that he attains:
by means of celestial chariots that travel everywhere and shine like ten million suns. (5.116)
[The city] was encircled by flower garlands, resounded with songs and instrumental music,
and filled with the sweet sounds of stringed instruments, while [the inhabitants] moved about at will, languid with pleasure.
Surrounded by Rudra-maidens, rare even to gods and dānavas, with yak-tail whisks being vigorously fanned and praised by gods and asuras alike. (5.118)
One may go to the divine city of Śiva, or wherever else may be pleasing; with whatever flowers, whether grown in water or on land, one should worship Śiva here.
Having worshipped with devotion using consecrated offerings, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
likewise, he who constructs a dense pavilion of flowers over Śiva [attains the same]. (5.120)
It was adorned with garlands and wreaths of flowers hanging down as far as the bases [of the vehicles], and with other marvelous great vehicles embellished with divine flowers. || 5.121 ||
Possessing all requisites and endowed with splendor, he shall go happily to the city of Śiva;
[he shall reach] his home adorned with fragrant flowers arranged in many forms.
Whoever should create [an image] radiant with various flowers on the auspicious festival days shall be surrounded by thousands of celestial chariots and other vehicles, all adorned with flowers.
Endowed with the pleasures of divine women and the delight of play,
he rejoices for an inexhaustible time, his commands unopposed by others.
He goes at will to all the worlds, beginning with that of Śiva, especially due to the performance of worship, the cultivation of devotion, and the arrangement of ritual offerings. (5.125)
Thus, the fruit should be understood in brief according to one's wealth.
Then, one should encircle the altar with garlands and worship the Liṅga.
Śiva, together with the Goddess and his son, rejoices through that practice;
the altar is the Goddess, and the Liṅga is Maheśvara himself. (5.127)
By worshipping those two, both the Goddess and the God become worshipped;
he who, having personally gathered flowers, worships Śiva correctly, [attains the fruit]. (5.128)

He who constantly honors Śiva with devotion by personally accepting those [offerings], and who establishes a grove for Śiva adorned with mangoes, bilva trees, and the like, [attains the highest state]. (5.129)
With *jātī*, *vijaya*, *rājārka*, *karavīra*, *abja*, and *kubjaka*; with *punnāga*, *nāga*, *vakula*, *aśoka*, *utpala*, and *campaka*. (5.130)
Listen to the merit of that [act] performed with plantains, golden ornaments, and so forth—[the merit equal to] as many leaves, flowers, seeds, sprouts, and fruits as there are. (5.131)
For that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
he who offers incense free from lac, resin, and oil even once to Śivā.
One shall become a knower of the four Vedas and attain birth [in a noble family], remaining constantly happy;
one should offer incense of black agallochum and camphor to Maheśvara. (5.133)
Listen to the fruit of his merit for practicing continuously for half a month:
for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Having enjoyed pleasures in the city of Śiva, at the end of that [period],
the Lord of the Earth directly receives guggulu mixed with clarified butter from Śaṅkara himself.
By giving even as much as half a māṣa, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
he who burns guggulu resin with clarified butter on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight for Śiva [attains the same]. (5.136)
Śaṅkara forgives thousands of offenses for him who offers devadāru, Meru, sarja, niryāsa, and kunduru.
By burning *śrīphala* mixed with clarified butter, one attains supreme prosperity;
by means of these fragrant substances, one performs incense-offerings that are six thousand times superior.
Ten thousand units of *agaru* and double that amount of black *agaru*;
ten thousand units of *gulgulu* and double that amount with clarified butter. (5.139)
One should always offer *priyaṅgu* and especially *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter;
specifically two thousand fruits of *māhiṣākṣa* *guggulu*.
By burning [an offering] mixed with clarified butter for one year, one becomes equal to Śiva;
likewise, by burning agarwood combined with ghee, or even bilva wood. (5.141)
A human being obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
he shall purify men joined with sin—of this there is no doubt. (5.142)
Incense produced from black agallochum is like fire to gold;
that devotion which anoints the inner city of Śiva with fragrant scents [is likewise]. (5.143)
One should cause the area from the door-panels and walls, extending horizontally and upwards along with the altar,
to be perfumed with flower garlands and especially with incense.
Listen to the merit of one who performs this even once:
they shall be fully endowed with all desires and possess thousands of Mahāyāna vehicles. (5.145)
Filling all directions with fragrant perfumes,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of kalpas.
At its conclusion, by the remainder of his merit, he shall become the sovereign of the three worlds;
and he who, with divine fragrances, adorns the abode of Śiva during both the Ṛta and Amṛta periods [shall likewise attain this].
Endowed with all these qualities, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
[The thread] made of silk or other materials may be black, yellow, or white. (5.148)
By giving a sacred thread to Rudra, one becomes a master of the Vedānta;
likewise by giving garments that are most variegated, substantial, and soft. (5.149)
Śiva would grant those which were indicated, unencased, and new;
indeed, as long as the measurement of the threads of the cloth was prescribed. (5.150)
For that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
even he who should give a liṅga made of gold, though only the size of a minute particle, [attains the same].
The seat of Indra lasts for as long as [the duration specified];
thus, in brief, the fruit should be understood according to one's wealth. (5.152)
For all the golden vessels and crowns in every respect, the meritorious bowl of *yorka* leaves, consecrated with the *madhuparka*, [is offered]. (5.153)
One should offer it to Śarva; he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One should prepare a prastha of śāli rice grains, making the food well-prepared.
One should offer that head to Śiva, especially on the fourteenth day;
likewise, one may offer turmeric, kṛsara, śaktu, pāyasa, and yāvaka.
If the food offering (naivedya) is well-prepared and mixed with pieces of sugar-cane,
then according to the number of grains of rice in that offering— || 5.156 ||
For as many thousands of yugas as there are balls of food made from pieces of sugar offered as an oblation, one is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 5.157 ||
The fruit of those cooked with ghee shall be a hundredfold greater than that of unrefined [grains].
For those who eat meat and fallen food, the fruit is traditionally held to be even greater still. (5.158)
Half of that amount should also be offered as scented water;
one should present well-ripened fruits such as the *mātuluṅga* and others. (5.159)
The fruit of offering edible foods to Śiva belongs to him who offers betel leaf accompanied by the five fragrant spices.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who offers it to Śiva and to the Guru:
his body shall be fragrant, radiant, and beautiful in every limb. (5.161)
By offering a lamp of ghee to Śiva that extends for a hundred yojanas, one is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of years.
Having transcended darkness, those who have fashioned a beautiful garland of lamps during the month of Kṛttikā travel in celestial chariots possessing the brilliance of the sun.
Indeed, on the fourteenth day or even on the full moon day, [he was] like ten thousand suns, illuminating the quarters with his splendor. || 5.164 ||
Seated in a celestial chariot that is a mass of radiance, having uplifted his entire lineage,
he remains until the number of lamps has been reached, having been awakened by being filled with ghee.
Having raised up a tall iron lamp-stand in the temple of Śiva, one is honored in the world of Rudra for as many thousands of yugas.
One obtains twice the merit compared to the former; there is no doubt about this.
One should carry a lamp upon one's head before Śiva day and night.
Or on the forehead, or with both hands joined upon the chest;
[he shall travel] in celestial chariots that go everywhere, resembling ten thousand suns in brilliance. (5.168)
One is honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred thousand divine aeons;
one should offer a mirror made of crystal before Śiva. (5.169)
Having adorned the perimeter with white garlands and sandalwood, he is glorious, fortunate, and capable of assuming any form at will, as pure as the rays of the moon. (5.170)
Having performed circumambulation of Śiva with devotion in both ways, a person is glorified in the world of Rudra for ten thousand times ten thousand kalpas.

One easily obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices through the remembrance and salutation [of Him]. This sacrifice of salutation and remembrance is the most auspicious of all sacrifices. (5.172)
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
having prostrated on the ground like a staff, one should worship him with such salutation.
And the destination that he attains cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices;
nor can that fruit which is obtained from all sacrifices, all fasts, and all sacred fords [be attained otherwise]. (5.174)
Through praise, recitation, and offerings, one shall obtain that fruit from Śiva;
or one should give a white, large banner, having fashioned it with five colors.
Adorned with the tinkling of small bells and graced by a peacock-feather parasol,
he stands above all the gods in a celestial chariot that reaches everywhere.
For a thousand manvantaras, he rejoices in heaven like Rudra;
banners, umbrellas, and celestial chariots are provided for him in all directions and intermediate points. (5.177)
And an eightfold array of great banners is also arranged in the cardinal and intermediate directions, together with a thousand celestial palaces, beautifully adorned with divine banners. (5.178)
For a hundred thousand divine aeons, he rejoices in heaven like Rudra, in a place as pure as the rays of the moon and adorned with networks of pearls. (5.179)
One should offer a parasol made of jeweled handles, or one adorned with gold;
with a beautiful and variegated parasol being held aloft, [the donor] shines.
Through the enjoyment of hundreds of celestial palaces, he shall go for a long time to the city of Śiva;
yet, if he should desire sovereignty, he may do so while still embodied at the end of his allotted lifespan.
He enjoys the earth, bounded by the ocean, under a single umbrella, yet bound by an iron chain and a great bell of loud sound. (5.182)
One should indeed bind [an image] made of bell-metal or iron in the temple of Śiva;
the illustrious Gaṇa Ghaṇṭākarṇa is exceedingly dear to Śiva. (5.183)
Endowed with power equal to that of Śiva, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
[He who offers] kettledrums, clay drums, trumpets, drums, and the like—|| 5.184 ||
He who offers musical instruments made of bamboo, bell-metal, and other materials to Śiva,
shall travel in celestial chariots that provide manifold enjoyments and resound with the sounds of flutes and lutes.
By the gift of women, music, and especially by that of dance, one is glorified in the world of Śiva for a hundred thousand divine ages.
In the world of Īśvara, he rejoices for an inexhaustible time according to his desire;
having offered a pair of conchs with a great, great sound in the abode of Śiva, [he attains this]. (5.187)
One is honored in the world of Rudra for ten million divine eons;
likewise, one who offers a canopy with the luster of a yellow lotus and adorned with *āmalaka* fruits [attains the same]. (5.188)
Adorned with garments of various colors or of a single hue, beautified by new clothes, equipped with small bells and tinkling ornaments, and further embellished with bodices. || 5.189 ||
Whoever places [an offering] upon Śiva or prepares it before him,
he rejoices in all the worlds like Rudra for ten million eons (yuga-koṭi).
Listen to the meritorious fruit for that illustrious person who would offer above Śiva a pavilion adorned with all kinds of gems and pearls. (5.191)
With tens of millions upon tens of millions of celestial palaces endowed with all objects of desire,
he dwells happily in the city of Śiva until the dissolution of all beings.
One should construct a sanctuary for Śarva, beautifully adorned with garments for worship—
either with fine silk, woven cloth, or divine emblems, or with cloths endowed with various colors.
For as many thousands of years as there are threads in the cloth or other woven fabrics, for that long one is honored in the world of Rudra.
The entire world is sustained by the oblation to Śiva through the gateway of creation;
by performing the fire-ritual while focusing upon that, the world becomes meritorious. (5.195)
Whoever should construct a most beautiful brick temple for the fire of Rudra would attain union with Rudra by performing the fire-rite there even once. || 5.196 ||
He who, having performed the Śiva-agnikārya for himself here with the triple life-span (triyāyuṣa),
is liberated from the ten sins by means of the white ashes of Śiva. (5.197)
Having prepared ten maṇḍalas at the edge of the temple of Śiva,
one who is endowed with all desired objects should constantly offer oblations (bali) upon them.
One should prepare [an offering] in a copper vessel, provided with flowers and incense,
for Rudra, the host of Mothers, and all the guardians of the directions.
Whoever performs this offering of bali even once toward the ten directions is honored in the world of Rudra for ten thousand years.
Having performed the fierce twilight offering (saṃdhyā-bali) daily, or on the festival days (parvan), at night,
one is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand aeons (kalpa).
A linga made of curd-rice, placed within a golden vessel or similar receptacle,
adorned with flowers and dūrvā grass, auspicious and beautifully decorated according to the prescribed ritual.
Carrying that vessel upon his head, he should walk slowly in a clockwise direction as far as the temple of Śiva, accompanied by the sounds of conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments.
Adorned with rows of banners and mirrors, graced by song, dance, and the like,
as well as by umbrellas, chowries, incense, and likewise by staff-lamps and other such offerings.
Standing before the liṅga, one should offer the remaining portion with curd and rice, mixed with flowers and unbroken grains, as a bali offering in all directions.
By this, may the fierce Mothers, Śiva, Umā, Ṣaṇmukha, and the others,
being pleased by this fierce offering, always grant me peace.

Removing the garlands of Śiva and wiping [the liṅga] at the conclusion of worship—each one of these acts alone would be equal [to the other], and one would obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (5.207) p. 47(73)
Having prepared a small *śiva*-maṇḍala measuring one cubit in front of Śiva, he should scatter it with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, or even leaves alone. (5.208)
By performing this once, a man becomes handsome, fortunate, illustrious, radiant, and happy like a god; he shall become a knower of the four Vedas in his very birth. (5.209)
Having thus beautified the ground in a temple of Śiva with svastikas, lotuses, and the like, using colored powders and flour-pastes, one shall obtain a hundredfold fruit. (5.210)
Having given sacrificial implements to Śiva, whether they be few or many,
he is honored in the world of Śiva according to his wealth.
What wonder is there that by giving [a gift] for the sake of Śiva—the cause of all causes—the donor receives an infinite fruit? (5.212)
Whatever is desired and excellent, and acquired through righteous means, should be offered to Śiva with devotion by those seeking infinite fruit. (5.213)

Even he who might act with deceitful intent toward a temple of Śiva at the proper time, by virtue of that very deed—though free from sin—he goes to heaven because of his [underlying] merit, despite the deceit. (5.214)
Beings employed in the construction of wells, gardens, food, drink, and so forth, as well as in the building of Śiva temples, or in tasks such as digging and uprooting; 5.215.
Even without desire, all things, both stationary and moving, go to heaven without doubt through the power of the Supreme Lord. (5.216)
A hundred cubits and more all around the *liṅga* is the sacred field (*kṣetra*) of Śiva;
for embodied beings, death there is the cause for attaining union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva. (5.217)
This measurement of the sacred field is traditionally recorded as being established by human-made *liṅgas*;
in a self-manifested (*svayambhū*) one, it would be a thousand [units], and in one made by a seer (*ārṣa*), it is half of that.
Since even one of evil conduct may go to the city of Śiva because of this [place], therefore one should construct a dwelling in the vicinity of a Śiva-field. (5.219)
The pure water situated in front of the Śivaliṅga should be known as the Śivagaṅgā; having bathed there, one shall go to Śiva. (5.220)
Whoever constructs a long pond or a well at a temple of Śiva,
together with twenty-one generations of their lineage, is honored in the world of Śiva.
Abandoning everything else and fixing his mind solely on Śiva, he who desires his own perfection should perform the ritual for the worship of Śiva. (5.222)
Life passes swiftly; youth passes swiftly;
even disease approaches swiftly. Therefore, Sadāśiva should always be worshipped.
As long as death does not arrive, as long as old age has not overtaken you, and as long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long worship Śaṅkara. (5.224)
"There is no other dharma equal to the worship of Śiva in the three worlds"—having realized this, one should always worship Sadāśiva with diligence. (5.225)
Those who, through devotion, [worship] Śiva—the Lord of the gods of gods, the peaceful, unborn, and sovereign—attain happiness in this world and go to the supreme state. (5.226)
Having worshipped the Lord of Creatures with a purified inner self, one should,
with palms joined in reverence, recite this hymn of praise out of devotion. (5.227)
I bow to Sadāśiva, the guide upon the path to Śiva.
I bow down to the eternal, beautiful, pure, teacher, purifier of faults, the Lord of the universe, the God Śaṅkara.
To the Lord who removes all sins, the auspicious one who removes all diseases,
the Sovereign God who grants boons, the Sovereign Lord who is the leader of mantras.
The man who hears this meritorious ritual of worship even once is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 5.231 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Merit of Materials for the Worship of Śiva," in the *Śivadharma-Uttara*, a scripture of the illustrious Śaiva tradition, proclaimed by Nandikeśvara.
Glorious One! Now begins the sixth chapter.
Śrī Nandikeśvara said: Beyond this, there is this secret [teaching] proclaimed by Rudra, which brings great prosperity,
pacifies all great disturbances, bestows great peace, and is auspicious.
It pacifies untimely death, wards off all diseases, subdues hostile armies, and always increases victory. (6.2)
It is always a means of paralyzing even an enemy's army and causing them to lose their composure;
it illuminates all the hosts of gods and planetary spirits as desired.
I shall explain, according to reality, the Dharma known as "The Chapter on Universal Peace.
[He is] three-eyed, bearing the crescent moon, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
Four-faced and four-armed, smeared with white ashes,
he is the most excellent, the one worthy of choice, the giver of boons, the God of gods, Maheśvara.
May the glorious one, who is bowed to by the three worlds, swiftly grant me peace;
she whose body is slender-waisted, with every limb being preeminent.
She is graced by a form that is yellowish-dark and exceedingly serene;
she is adorned with a tilaka on her forehead and bears the crescent of the moon.
The goddess was clad in divine garments and adorned with all ornaments;
she was the great abode of beauty and virtue among all excellent women and all womankind.
The goddess Umā, the bestower of boons, who is satisfied with mere meditation,
came in person with a peaceful form and immeasurable splendor. (6.9)

May she who is pleased with her devotees and affectionate toward those who are devoted grant me peace— she who possesses the luster of a ruby, who is gentle, and who is adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Though not a child, he appears in the form of a child; he has six faces and rides upon a peacock.
With a face like the full moon, he is gentle and endowed with the power of the three auspicious Śivas.
Born from the limbs of Kṛttikā, Umā, and Agni, honored by the gods,
the immensely radiant Kārttikeya is solely intent upon the granting of boons.
May he grant me constant peace, and may he always bestow strength and happiness upon me—
he who is clothed in white garments, three-eyed, and possesses the luster of gold.
May the trident-bearing Nandīśa, possessed of great wisdom and permeated by Śiva,
grant me peace and an excellent mind directed toward dharma.
Large-bellied and massive-bodied, with a luster like smooth collyrium, the god has a single prominent tusk; he is elephant-faced and possesses great strength.
Adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread and decorated with serpent ornaments,
he is the support of all prosperity, the leader of the Gaṇas, and the bestower of boons.
May the divine son of Rudra, the leader and the remover of obstacles, always grant me great peace and supreme accomplishment. (6.17)
Resembling a deep blue sapphire, three-eyed, with a blazing trident raised as his weapon,
wearing red garments, glorious, and adorned with black-bodied serpents.
May Mahākāla, possessed of great power, grant me supreme peace— he who is incomparable in the removal of evil and the destroyer of misfortune and impurity. (6.19)
With the luster of the color of a conch, jasmine, and the moon, and with a neck possessing the brilliance of emerald,
he was fierce and held a rosary of beads, standing like Viṣṇu himself.
Four-faced, four-armed, three-eyed, and eternally radiant;
the lord of the earth, the bull, righteousness (dharma), the most excellent among all that is most excellent. (6.21)
He bears the Lord upon his back; therefore, Dharma is the master of the world.
May the illustrious Bull, the bearer of the bull, grant me peace. (6.22)
The omniscient one, equal to all, all-pervading, born from the head, the Lord, the subduer of enemy armies, the Teacher—may he grant me peace. (6.23)
Clad in yellow garments, in the form of a maiden, indeed well-adorned;
the Mother of the Gaṇas, Ambikā, the three-eyed one, the auspicious Gaurī, the Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī). 6-24.
May the Goddess, who grants all accomplishments and is supremely devoted to grace, my Mother, bestow peace upon me and swiftly grant me success. (6.25)
With a fleshless body, its tendons and bones firmly bound together, exceedingly subtle and transcendent, the great Bhṛṅgiriṭi possesses three eyes. (6.26)
May that great hero, the son of Rudra, whose mind is solely devoted to Rudra, also swiftly bestow peace through his tranquil nature. (6.27)
The Lord Caṇḍeśvara has three eyes; he wields a great battle-axe and holds a rosary in his hand, accompanied by a fierce host of attendants.
May the Great Yogin, who removes fierce evil and purifies even the sin of killing a Brahmin, grant me supreme and auspicious well-being. (6.29)
Seated in the lotus posture, resembling a lotus, with four lotus-like faces, holding a water-pot, glorious, and worshipped by the Siddhas and Gandharvas. || 6.30 ||
Constantly devoted to the meditation on Śiva and proficient in the true nature of Śiva,
may Brahmā, through the divine word "Brahman," grant me peace.
Seated upon Tārkṣya, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
