dark-complexioned, wearing yellow garments, and adorned with a forest garland.
The god Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, the supreme deity among those worthy of sacrifice,
was endowed with the grace of Śiva and devoted to the meditation upon Śiva.
May the illustrious Viṣṇu, devoted to the worship of Śiva, grant me peace;
may the Goddess, who resembles a ruby and whose face is a four-petalled lotus, [grant me peace].
With her hand adorned by a rosary and holding a water-pot,
the auspicious Brahmāṇī has a gentle countenance and is devoted to the worship of Śiva.
May the goddess, who resembles the snowy mountain and is borne by a great bull, being pleased, always grant me peace through the sound of the Veda.
Holding a trident in her hand, she bestows boons, adorned with serpent ornaments;
she is a devotee of Rudra, possessed of great heroism, and ever intent upon the worship of Rudra.
Four-armed, four-faced, and three-eyed, the remover of sins—may the eternally radiant Goddess of Maheśa, being pleased, take away my distress. (6.38)
The goddess whose vehicle is a peacock has a body as red as vermilion;
she holds a spear in her hand, possesses great heroism, and is adorned with all ornaments. (6.39)
The Great Goddess, devoted to Rudra and ever intent upon the worship of Rudra—may that goddess Kaumārī, the bestower of boons, swiftly grant me peace. (6.40)
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in her hands, fond of dark blue and yellow garments,
four-armed, mounted upon Garuḍa, Vaiṣṇavī is worshipped by the gods.
Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, with her mind solely fixed on Rudra,
may she who crushes all Asuras grant me perpetual peace.
She has the formidable snout of a boar, she rides upon an excellent boar,
she possesses a dark luster, she grants all boons, and her weapons are the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Constantly threatening obstacles and always worshipping Sadāśiva, may the boon-granting goddess Vārāhī bestow upon me forgiveness and health. (6.144)
Mounted upon Airāvata, with a curved trunk, she is possessed of great strength;
adorned with a thousand eyes, she possesses the luster of gold.
Worshipped by the Siddhas and Gandharvas, adorned with every ornament, may the goddess Aindrī always swiftly bestow peace upon me. (6.46)
With hair standing erect, fierce, and dark-complexioned; fleshless, bound together by sinews;
with a gaping mouth and a terrifying countenance, she wields a sword and a shield.
The goddess Kapālamālinī is fierce, bearing a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga);
her eyes are reddish-brown, and she is draped in an elephant hide.
Her limbs are entwined by various serpents; she dwells in the abode of the pretas;
in the form of Śiva, she is fierce, terrible, and fearsome. (6.49)
May Cāmuṇḍā, in her fierce form and seated upon a variegated mechanical throne,
grant me protection here from ghosts, spirits, and goblins.
The divine Mothers of Space and likewise the other Mothers of the World bring long life, prosperity, strength, happiness, fame, and the glory of increasing fortune. (6.51)
All the Mothers of beings, as well as the other Mother-goddesses of the gods—
the great goddesses who are the mothers of all— stand with their own weapons grasped in their hands.
Pervading the world, they abide there; desiring offerings, large-bellied, devoted to Rudra, possessed of great heroism, fierce, and intent on the worship of Rudra.
May the Mothers, worshipped by the gods, grant me constant peace;
and those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes.
The Mothers who have the form of Rudras, those who are the lords of the Gaṇas, and others who have become obstacles, residing in the ten directions; || 6.55 ||
May all, with joyful minds, accept this offering;
may they swiftly grant me success and always protect me from fears.
In the eastern direction, there are those hosts who hold vajras in their hands and possess great strength;
they have very white eyes, appear white, and are likewise white and red.
May those dwelling in heaven, the atmosphere, and on earth, as well as those residing in the depths of the netherworld—
who are devoted to the worship of Rudra— joyfully grant me peace at all times.
And in the southeast, all the Gaṇas have sacrificial ladles in their hands and carry quivers;
they have deep red eyes, appear red-hued, and likewise possess blood-red glances.
May those dwelling in heaven, the atmosphere, and on earth, as well as those residing in the depths of the netherworld,
who are devoted to the worship of the Supreme Lord, grant supreme well-being.
In the northwest are those hosts who always hold banners in their hands;
they have beautiful lotus-like eyes, resemble lotuses, and are as red as lotuses.

May those dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth, as well as those residing in the depths of Pātāla, who are devoted to the worship of the Supreme Lord, always grant me peace. (6.62)
All those hosts belonging to Kaubērī, who constantly hold treasures in their hands, have beautiful yellow eyes; they are yellowish in appearance, as well as yellowish-red.
May those dwelling in heaven, the atmosphere, and on earth, as well as those residing in the depths of the netherworld—who are devoted to the worship of the Supreme Lord—always grant me peace. (6.64)
In the northeast, however, are those Gaṇas who are peaceful and wield tridents;
they have very subtle eyes, appear subtle, and are likewise subtly red.
May those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld, being ever intent upon the worship of Śiva, grant me constant well-being. (6.66)
Those hosts who belong to the lower region are constantly armed with discuses;
they have very smoky eyes, resemble smoke, and are indeed smoke-red in hue.
May those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on earth, as well as those residing in the depths of Pātāla, who are intent upon the worship of Śiva, always grant me peace. (6.68)
But those groups who dwell in the upper realms always hold lotuses in their hands;
they are Susūkṣmas, Sūkṣmas, and likewise Sūkṣmalohitas. (6.69)
May those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on the earth, as well as those residing in the depths of the netherworld, who are intent upon the worship of Śiva, always grant me peace. (6-70)
These hosts are high-souled and possessed of great strength;
having worshipped Śiva with diligence, one should offer them their sacrificial oblation (bali).
Then, with well-pleased minds, may they always grant me peace;
they are situated in the eastern part of the city named Amarāvatī.
It was crowded with hosts of Vidyādharas, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
encased in jeweled ramparts, and adorned with great gems.
There, the glorious lord of the gods, wielder of the thunderbolt and possessed of great strength, shines resplendent with his beautiful thousand eyes. (6.74)
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, golden-hued and of great splendor, the Lord of the Devas is ever joyful and devoted to the worship of the Supreme Lord. (6.75)
Sufficiently devoted solely to the meditation on Śiva and endowed with devotion to Śiva,
he was accompanied by other devotees of Śiva as well as by the gods along with their followers.
Devoted to the prostration of Śiva, may he perform my rite of pacification (śāntika).
In the southeastern quarter, however, lies the auspicious city of Tejovatī.
It was crowded with various deities and filled with the blazing radiance of jewels;
there, his limbs were enveloped in flames, possessing a luster like glowing embers from a lamp.
The god Agni brings prosperity to embodied beings and destroys their sins;
he is intent on the worship of Śiva and the recitation of mantras, purified by the constant remembrance of Śiva. (6.79)
May the Lord grant me peace as well as the complete destruction of my sins;
there stands to the south the city named Vaivasvatapurī.
Enclosed by an iron wall and adorned with palaces,
he stands in the center of each of those [cities], situated within a mansion and granting all desires.
There, the abode of the hosts of gods and asuras, of the ancestors, yakṣas, and uragas,
was filled with one who resembled a sapphire, with long eyes whose corners were red.
Mounted upon a great buffalo, adorned with black garlands, garments, and ornaments, the glorious Yama,
possessed of great majesty, is devoted to the dharma of Śiva.
May he who is intent upon the worship of Śiva grant me security and health.
In the south-western direction, in the region of Śiśu, is the auspicious city of Kṛṣṇāvatī.
It was crowded with hosts of great rākṣasas and teeming with piśācas and pretas;
there stood one resembling a cloud, adorned with black garlands, garments, and ornaments.
The Lord of the Rakshasas, Nairrita, possesses great splendor; he holds a sword in his hand, has a formidable face, and is radiant. He is eternally and always devoted to the worship of Shiva.
May he, eager for devotion to Śiva, grant me great peace.
In the western quarter, however, is the auspicious city Śuddhavatī.
It was strewn with various jewels and crowded with various kinnaras;
there, [he was] like a pearl, with deep reddish-brown eyes.
Clad in white garments, holding a noose in his hand, and possessed of great strength—Varuṇa [is thus described]. With supreme devotion, his mind is fixed solely upon Śiva. (6–89)
May they utterly destroy my fear of disease, grief, affliction, and torment.
In the northwestern quarter lies the auspicious city Gandhavatī.
Crowded with hosts of sages and Siddhas, it has golden ramparts and archways;
there, [the city] is made of copper and iron, and is dark-brown and red.
Since he has the sky as his pervasive abode, is absorbed within the intermediate space, and possesses the staff of the banner as his weapon,
Pavana is the supreme deity, permeated by the nature of the Supreme Lord.
May it constantly grant me security, health, strength, and peace;
it is called Mahodadhipurī, and it is exceedingly radiant in the north.
It was crowded with many yakṣas, adorned with various jewels,
and enclosed by walls of gold as well as walls of precious gems.
There the god stood, mace in hand, adorned with variegated garlands, garments, and ornaments;
he was short-armed, possessed of great splendor, and had deep reddish-brown eyes.
May the glorious Kubera, the giver of boons, who is devoted to the worship of Hara’s feet, being pleased and tranquil with a peaceful mind, grant me peace. (6.96)
The beautiful city of Yaśovatī is situated in the northeastern direction;
it is filled with various hosts of attendants and contains divine abodes of many kinds of jewels.
Extending as far as the wall of light, incomparable and ever-shining, there [stood one] resembling a pearl, with the moon made into his crest-ornament. (6.98)
The three-eyed Hara, whose limbs possess a tranquil form and who holds a rosary of beads,
is Īśāna, the supreme deity, the highest among all the best of gods. (6.99)
May he too, with his entire being, swiftly grant me peace—
those who dwell in the world of earth (bhūrloka), the world of atmosphere (bhuvarloka), and the heavenly world (svargaloka).
May the gods, endowed with divine radiance, who reside in the Maharloka, Janaloka, and Tapoloka, always grant me peace.
May those joyful gods also always grant me peace;
and those gods in Janaloka who possess the luster of polished gold.
May those gods who eternally bow to Īśāna and who reside in their radiant celestial chariots in Maharloka always grant me peace. (6.103)
May those gods who abide in the heavenly realm, radiant and of great brilliance, always destroy fear for those most intent on bowing to Bhava.
May those gods who, illuminating the ten directions, reside in the world of mortals, always bowing to Śaṅkara, grant me victory. (6.105)
May those who dwell in mountain caves, difficult terrains, and forests, with their minds fixed solely on Śiva, pacify my sins.
May those who are constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra always grant me peace,
with bodies as white as the rays of the autumnal moon and endowed with stainless luster.
May Sarasvatī, who is devoted to Śiva, who possesses the luster of beautiful gold and has hands like lotus-buds, swiftly grant me peace.
And the illustrious goddess Śrīdevī, devoted to Śiva, may she grant me prosperity; she who is radiant with variegated gold and possesses a beautiful moon-like face. (6-109)
May Jayādevī, who is devoted to Śiva and wears a radiant golden girdle with a most wonderful necklace, grant all my desires.
May the devotee of Śiva, who has conquered all, grant me victory—she whose limbs are red as vermilion and whose eyes extend as far as her ears. (6.111)
Endowed with a multitude of rays, drawn by the seven-horsed chariot,
the Lord Garbhastimālī is devoted to the worship of the feet of Hara.
May he grant me great peace and dispel the affliction of the planetary spirits; may the tawny-eyed one, with a complexion like a ruby, protect my body.
Aṅgāraka was a devotee of Śiva, dedicated to the worship of Rudra;
he was endowed with the true nature of Rudra, his mind fixed solely on the meditation of Rudra.
May he, adorned with a glorious body having the hue of saffron, always destroy all fear and affliction caused by the planets for me.
May the wise and illustrious devotee of Śiva dispel the affliction caused by the planets—he who possesses the luster of molten gold and is the abode of all knowledge. (6.116)
Bṛhaspati was at all times devoted to the worship of Īśāna;
he too, with a peaceful mind and through supreme meditative absorption (samādhi), [practiced].
Having completely conquered the affliction of the planets, may he grant me victory—
he who possesses the luster of snow, kunda flowers, and the moon, and is worshipped by the lords of both gods and daityas.
May Śukra, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel the affliction caused by the planets;
he who resembles a dark blue cloud and possesses the luster of deep red eyes. (6-119)
May Śanaiścara, who is devoted to Śiva, dispel the affliction caused by the planets;
he is the son of Siṃhikā, possessing the hue of a dark cloud or collyrium, and endowed with great strength.
May Rāhu, who is intent on the worship of Śiva, dispel the affliction caused by the planets—he who possesses a smoky body, is cruel, and is accompanied by all portents of calamity. || 6-121 ||
May Ketu, devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel the affliction caused by the planets;
for these great-souled planets are always intent upon the worship of Śiva.
May those who always desire my welfare grant me peace at all times—she whose mouth holds death, the one of great power named Vṛṣṭi. (6.123)
May she who is fair-faced, the dispeller of obstacles, the bestower of nourishment, and the bringer of victory—she who is devoted to bowing before Rudra—swiftly grant me peace. (6.124)
The third, the seventh, the tenth, and the fourteenth;
likewise the fourth, the eighth, the eleventh, and the full moon day. (6.125)
May these auspicious ones, who cause the removal of obstacles and arise from both the white and the black, constantly destroy fear and grant me victory. (6.126)
The new moon day (amāvāsyā) is greatly meritorious and is attended by the ancestors and the gods;
it is indeed peaceful, supreme, and most dear to Śiva. (6.127)
Endowed with the splendor of Śiva, may she grant me peace;
the first lunar day is conjoined with Fire, and the second has the presiding deity as its lord.
The third is of great merit and is accompanied by the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada);
the fourth is of great merit and has the elephant-faced deity as its presiding divinity.
The fifth [tithi] is eternally endowed with Śrī; the sixth has Skanda as its presiding deity;
the seventh is indeed conjoined with the Sun; and the eighth has Rudra as its presiding deity.
The ninth lunar day is extremely fierce, with the goddess Durgā as its presiding deity;
the tenth is conjoined with Yama, and the eleventh is joined with Indra.
The twelfth day is conjoined with Viṣṇu; the thirteenth day with Madana;
the fourteenth day with Maheśa; and the full moon day with the Moon.
May all these lunar days, devoted to the worship of Īśāna and intent on my welfare, grant me peace at all times and forever.
Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Atigaṇḍa, Sukarman, Dhṛti, and likewise Śūla; (6-134)
Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Vyāghāta, and likewise Harṣaṇa; Vajra, Siddhi, Vyatīpāta, Varīyān, Parigha, and Śiva. (6.135)
Siddha, Sādhya, Śubha, Śubhra, Brāhma, Māhendra, and Vaidhṛti—these powerful yogas indeed arise from the Moon and the Sun. (6.136)
May all these people, who are devoted to Śiva’s bhakti, who perform the rites of Śiva’s bhakti, and who are intent on the worship of Śiva, perform my śāntika rite. (6.137)
Kṛttikā is the supreme goddess; Rohiṇī has a beautiful countenance;
Mṛgaśiras is glorious; and Ārdrā is most radiant.
Punarvasu, as well as Puṣya and Āśleṣā, are of great power;
for these are the Mothers of the Nakṣatras, illuminating with garlands of light. (6.139)
Devoted to the worship of Mahādeva and empowered by the majesty of Mahādeva,
may these goddesses stationed in the eastern quarter always grant me peace.
Makhā is endowed with all virtues, as is Pūrvaphālgunī;
Uttaraphālgunī is excellent, and likewise Hastā and Citrā are supreme. (6.141)
Svāti and Viśākhā, bestowers of boons, stationed in the southern positions,
always worship the supreme deity at all times.
Impelled by Śiva, may these also perform pacification for me:
Anurādhā, as well as Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūlā, endowed with the power of supernatural success.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā is of great power, and Uttarāṣāḍhā is auspicious;
the lunar mansion named Abhijit and Śravaṇa are supremely radiant.
These women, radiant from behind, shining and beautiful in form, worship Īśāna at all times, being well-disposed toward him. (6.145)
May they, being pleased and composed, grant me peace and prosperity during the asterisms of Śraviṣṭhā,
Śatabhiṣaj, and likewise Pūrvabhādrapadā.
Revatī, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Aśvinī possess great supernatural power; Bharaṇī possesses great heroism; these are always situated in the north. (6.147)
Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, with their minds solely intent on the meditation of Śiva, may they grant me perpetual peace, strength, and good fortune. (6.148)
And Kanyā is the supreme goddess, and Makara possesses great supernatural power;
and Ṛṣabha is of great heroism, well-cultivated in the state of auspiciousness. || 6.149 ||
These [deities] on the southern side always worship Sadāśiva with supreme devotion; may they always grant me peace. (6-150)
Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius are situated in the west;
may those devoted to the worship and adoration of Śiva always grant me peace. (6.151)
Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces—these are situated in the north;
they always worship Rudra, the leader of the world.
May the seven renowned and supremely radiant sages, culminating in Dhruva, who are ever devoted to meditation upon Rudra, grant me constant peace. (6.153)
May Kāśyapa, Gālava, Gārgya, and the great sage Viśvāmitra, endowed with the grace of Śiva, always grant me peace. (6.154)
Manu, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Mārkaṇḍeya, Pulaha, Kratu, Nārada, Bhṛgu, Ātreya, Bhāradvāja, and the sage Aṅgiras. (6.155)
Śālmali, Kauśika, Kaṇva, Śākalya, Punarvasu,
and Śālaṅkāyana— these were sages of great asceticism.
May the wives of the sages, who are highly meritorious, and the daughters and sons of the sages—who are ever intent on meditation upon and worship of Śiva—grant me peace at all times. (6.157)
May those who are constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva always grant me peace;
as well as the Siddhas whose austerities have been perfected, and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The Vidyādharas, the Garuḍas, and the great Ṛṣis are devoted to Maheśvara; they worship the station of Maheśvara. (6-159)
May those who are devoted to the dharma of Śiva swiftly grant success!
[There are] Namuci, the king of the Daityas, and the very powerful Śaṅkukarṇa.
Jambha, Nikumbha, and Śakaṭa— these high-souled Daityas were solely devoted to the worship of Śiva and were permeated by the true nature of Śiva.
May they bestow nourishment, strength, and valor that brings about happiness.
There was a Daitya of supreme heroism, renowned as the great Nāga Aśvavikhyāta. (6.162)
Constantly devoted to the worship of the god Hāṭakeśvara,
may you, who possess great supernatural power, swiftly bestow upon me strength and heroism.
Mahājambha, Hayagrīva, Prahlāda the foremost of the Daityas,
the Daityas headed by Tārakākṣa, and the high-souled Kālanemi.
Vairocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, Suparvan, Sulomaka, Mucukunda, Sukunda, and likewise the Daitya Rocanaka. (6.165)
With supreme devotion, they always quickly worship Śiva;
may they always grant me nourishment through their nature as Sadāśiva.
May the highly fortunate wives of the Daityas, the auspicious daughters of the Daityas, and the sons of the Daityas always grant me peace. (6.167)
With a reddish body and long eyes with red corners, he displays the majesty produced by great prosperity and is marked with the signs of the conch and the lotus. || 6.168 ||
May Ananta, the king of the Naga lords, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet,
destroy the poison of great sins and swiftly grant me peace. (6.169)
With a body that was perfectly white, he had a crest of brilliantly white stones; he displayed the majestic pride of lovely serpents and was beautifully adorned like Hara.
May Vāsuki, the lord of the Naga kings, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet, destroy the poison of great sins and grant me security and health. (6-171)
With a body exceedingly beautiful, with abundant wealth for enjoyment,
and with a brilliance most radiant, he was marked with the auspicious svastika sign.
May the glorious Takṣaka, the lord of nāgas, whose splendor is equal to ten million nāgas,
grant me great peace and the destruction of all defects.
With an exceedingly dark complexion and a head formidable with matted locks, he is endowed with three lines upon his neck and has uplifted terrible fangs as weapons.
May Kārkoṭaka, of great splendor and endowed with pride in his venom, having suddenly neutralized fierce poisons, grant me peace. (6.175)
With a body the color of a lotus and beautiful, lotus-like eyes,
he bore the auspicious mark of a lotus-stalk scar upon his neck.
The renowned Padma, who possesses great wealth and is devoted to the worship of Hara’s feet, may he perform [this] great peace (*mahāśānti*) which destroys the great sins... || 6-177 ||
Nor was Puṇḍarīka ever adorned on his head with a conch, trident, or lotus, though he possessed immeasurable splendor. (6.178)
Mahāpadma, who possesses great enjoyment and is eternally devoted to Paśupati,
having destroyed terrible poison, may he swiftly grant me peace. (6-179)
Dark-complexioned, adorned with bodily ornaments, glorious, and lotus-eyed,
he was intoxicated by the pride of his poison and strength, and possessed a single line upon his neck.
Radiant with the power of the conch-shell hair-tuft, a worshiper of the lotus feet of Śiva, may he destroy most terrible poison and perform a rite of peace for me. (6.181)
With a body exceedingly white, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
adorned with a serpent whose coils were radiant, he was marked by the characteristic signs of Śambhu.
The lord of serpents named Gulika is eternally devoted to Hara;
having removed my terrible poison, may he perform my pacification. (6.183)
And those nāgas who are in the atmosphere, those nāgas who dwell in heaven, and those nāgas who reside on the earth in mountain caves and difficult terrains. || 6.184 ||
May all the Nāgas who dwell in Pātāla, being fully concentrated here and intent upon the worship of Rudra’s feet, always grant me peace. (6.185)
May the female nāgas, the nāga maidens, and likewise the young nāgas—devoted to Śiva and well-disposed—always grant me peace. (6.186)
Whoever recites or hears this description of the Nāga, serpents shall not harm them, nor shall their venom affect them. (6.187)
One constantly obtains whatever is thought of, as well as the complete destruction of evil; they swiftly bestow accomplishment, free from all obstacles. (6.188)
The Gaṅgā, the meritorious great goddess, the Yamunā, and the river Narmadā; also the Gomatī, the Kāverī, the Varuṇā, and likewise the Devikā. (6-189)
The great rivers, permeated by the true being of Śiva, worship the Lord who is the master of all beings, the Supreme Lord, the Great Īśvara.
May they grant me constant peace as well as the complete destruction of my sins;
may they swiftly bestow accomplishment that destroys all evil.
The Candrabhāgā, the highly meritorious river Godāvarī, the auspicious Sarayū, the excellent Gaṇḍakī, the Kauśikī, and the Sarasvatī. (6.192)
May these rivers, which are greatly meritorious and devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet, grant me constant peace, their minds fixed solely on meditation upon Śiva. (6.193)
The river named Nairañjanā, the great river Śoṇa, and the supreme, auspicious Mandākinī are likewise situated there.
May these and other rivers—those on earth and those flowing through the divine atmosphere—who are devoted to the worship of Rudra, always grant me peace. (6.195)
May those secret holy places, as well as the lakes extending to the ocean,
all presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha, perform the rite of pacification.
The god Mahāvaiśravaṇa, king of the yakṣas, possesses great supernormal power;
he is surrounded by ten million yakṣas and accompanied by an incalculable number of yakṣas. || 6-197 ||
Endowed with great prosperity, he was devoted to the worship of Hara’s feet;
he was solely intent on meditation upon Śiva and was the most excellent among those who delight in Hara’s feet.
May the great yakṣa Māṇibhadra, adorned with precious jewels, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, being well-pleased, grant me peace. (6.199)
With a captivating necklace clinging to her neck,
the Yakṣiṇī shines, her form surrounded by Yakṣa maidens.
Dedicated to the worship and adoration of Śiva, may he perform my pacification;
he is the lord of Yakṣas named Pāñcika, resplendent with earrings and bracelets. (6.201)
He shines with a variegated crown and two armlets;
he is joined by innumerable yakṣas and accompanied by ten million yakṣas.
May the illustrious Yakṣa Vibhaṇḍaka, adorned with various jewels and ever intent on the worship of Hara, perform my pacification rite.
Karna always shines with beautiful earrings;
he is the lord of the Yakṣas, the master of the Yakṣas, the wise commander of the Yakṣa army.
May Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of great splendor, the Yakṣa and sovereign of the Yakṣas, who is devoted to the worship of the feet of Hara, perform peace for me. (6.205)
Clothed in divine silken garments and adorned with jewels and gold,
he was a devotee of Śiva, meditating upon Śiva, and entirely devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Endowed with the grace of Śiva, may the great yakṣa Pūrṇabhadra, adorned with all ornaments, perform my rite of pacification.
He shines with a golden band adorned with the luster of jewels,
his form surrounded by thousands of millions of yakṣas.
Devoted to prostrating before Rudra, always delighting in devotion to Rudra,
and intent upon the worship of Rudra, may he perform my rite of pacification. (6.209)
And Virūpākṣa, the lord of the Yakṣas, clothed in white garments and possessed of great splendor,
was accompanied by beautiful golden garlands and the tinkling sound of small bells.
Always adorned and solely intent upon granting boons, and eternally devoted to the worship of Rudra, may he perform my propitiatory rite. (6.211)
And those yakṣas who are in the intermediate space, those yakṣas who dwell in heaven, and those yakṣas who inhabit mountain caves and difficult terrains; || 6-212 ||
The yakṣas dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), who assume various forms and brandish uplifted weapons,
are devotees of Śiva, well-disposed, and eager for the worship of Śiva.
May the Yakṣiṇīs of various forms, as well as the Yakṣa youths—joyful, peaceful, and devoted to peace—grant me tranquility. (6.214)
The Yakṣa maidens of great enjoyment, through the meditation on Śiva, [attain] peace, well-being, security, strength, and supreme auspiciousness. (6.215)
May all the mountains everywhere, and all the mountains of great supernatural power, being ever composed, swiftly grant success. (6.216)
May all those who are devoted to Śiva, being well-disposed, always grant me security—both all the oceans everywhere and whatever other oceans exist upon the earth. (6.217)
May all the Rākṣasas everywhere, even those of terrible form, be constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra and perform my pacification.
Those Rākṣasas who are of great heroism and those Rākṣasas who possess great strength—
those Rākṣasas who dwell in the water and those Rākṣasas who are in the intermediate space (antarikṣa). || 6-219 ||
May those Rākṣasas of Pātāla who are constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra, being perpetually permeated by Śiva, grant me constant peace. (6.220)
May the splendor of that god, whose form is Bhairava and who is smeared with the ashes of the deceased, always grant me peace. (6.221)
Then there were yoginīs of great power, always resplendent in their attire,
as well as ḍākinīs of great supernatural might who assumed many forms.
May those who are devoted to bowing to Rudra, who are always delighted by the worship of Rudra, and whose minds are solely fixed on Rudra, always grant me peace. (6.223)
The ḍākinīs who have gone into the intermediate space and those residing in heaven,
those in the netherworld and on the surface of the earth, and those who dwell in mountain fastnesses— || 6.224 ||
May the three eyes of that god, whose trident is radiant, always grant me peace through his splendor.
All beings are of great form; all beings are most radiant;
all beings who are present here, and those others who are elsewhere.
And those beings who are in the intermediate space, those beings who are established in heaven,
and those beings on the surface of the earth and in the netherworld who bring about the occurrence of events— || 6.227 ||
May the splendor of that deity, who holds a stainless khaṭvāṅga and a trident in his sprout-like hands, always grant me peace.

The hungry ghosts (preta), all the hosts of hungry ghosts, those hungry ghosts who face in every direction, those hungry ghosts who are exceedingly radiant, and those hungry ghosts who feed on blood. || 6.229 ||

And those pretas who are in the intermediate space, those pretas who reside in heaven, the pretas in the netherworld and on the surface of the earth, and those pretas who can assume any form at will; || 6.230 ||
All the Piśācas, possessing superior qualities, assume various forms;
those Piśācas who are in the intermediate space and those Piśācas who are in heaven.
Those piśācas on the surface of the earth who possess many forms and move with the speed of thought—
[he] for whom the half-moon is his crest-jewel and whose ornament is ashes.
By the splendor of that deity, may all seizures of epilepsy and all seizures of fever always bring peace to me.

Those who are the spirits of fetuses and children, those who are the spirits of various diseases, those who are the spirits in the intermediate space, and those who are the supreme spirits in heaven; || 6-234 ||
Those who are in the netherworld and on the surface of the earth, and those grahas in every direction—
[he] whose throat is great blue, and whose ornaments are serpents.
"By the splendor of that deity, may they always grant me peace"—thus did all the gods and others, who carry out the commands of Śiva. (6.236)
"May they always bring peace to the world and to the devotees of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, he stood with palms joined in reverence in the presence of the God of gods.
Becoming intent on the meditation of Śiva and uttering this hymn with devotion:
"Victory to you who are established in the yoga of the Self! Victory to you whose mind is perfectly perfected! (6.238)
Homage be to you, O Lord of Victory, the sole hero among those who grant victory;
victory to the supreme deity, victory to the one of auspicious renown! (6.239)
Victory to You whose form is manifest; salutations to You who have conquered all that is to be recited.
Victory to the ordainer of Lakṣmī; victory to the bestower of splendor!
Victory to you, the pure in speech; salutations again and again to the Unconquered!
Worship him who holds the trident in his hand; victory to the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff!
Victory to you who have conquered the worlds; victory to you, whose form is beauty, salutations to you!
Victory to you whose body is half-consort; victory to you who bear the crescent moon!
Victory to the God, the Lord of the three gods; victory to you, Rudra, salutations!
Victory to the Lord of the three worlds; victory to the one of renowned fame!
Salutations to you, Śarva, the support of victory and the creator of victory; victory to you of the stainless body, victory to the accomplisher of all aims!
"Victory to the destroyer of Manmatha! Salutations to you, O Īśāna!"—whoever thus recites or likewise hears this chapter on peace (Śāntikādhyāya), [attains the highest state].
Having shaken off all sins, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
one desiring a daughter obtains a daughter, and one desiring victory shall obtain victory.
One who desires wealth shall obtain wealth; one who desires a son shall obtain sons; a seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge; and a seeker of yoga shall attain yoga. (6.247)
Whatever desires a person may pray for here through hearing [this teaching], they shall all quickly attain; moreover, such a person becomes beloved by the gods. || 6-248 ||
Having heard this meritorious chapter, if a man enters into battle,
he shall conquer all his enemies and be filled with auspicious blessings. (6.249)
He rejoices for an inexhaustible time, while another who follows that teaching is not overcome by diseases and is established with sons and grandsons.
Having heard this meritorious chapter, whatever man recites it for the sake of another,
the diseases arising from wind, bile, and other humors shall not afflict him.
For him there is no untimely death, nor is he bitten by snakes;
poison does not course through his body, and he suffers neither dullness, blindness, nor muteness. (6.252)
For him there shall be no fear of calamities, nor shall there be any fear of portents;
he is never defiled by the faults caused by malevolent spells.
Whatever merit belongs to all sacred fords, especially those such as the Gaṅgā,
one obtains that merit multiplied ten millionfold by listening to this here.
By hearing this, one obtains the fruit of ten Rājasūya sacrifices and a hundred Agniṣṭomas, multiplied by ten million times ten million.
He shall be invulnerable to all the gods and especially to others;
free from all diseases, he shall live for more than a hundred years.
The killer of a cow, the ungrateful person, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the guru’s bed, the murderer of one who has sought refuge, and the betrayer of a friend’s trust. (6.257)
Even one who has committed wicked sins, such as a matricide or a patricide,
is liberated from all misdeeds through the mere disposition of hearing this. (6.258)
One should not give this meritorious chapter on peace to just anyone;
it was declared by Śiva in the past that it is to be bestowed only upon a devotee of Śiva.
He who recites this day after day shall be eternally endowed with power, free from the obstruction of powers, and fulfilled in all his desires. (6.260)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Recitation for Peace," in the *Śivadharmottara*, a treatise on the *Śivadharma* proclaimed by Nandikeśvara.
Śrī. Now begins the seventh chapter.
Salutation to Śiva.
Nandikeśvara said:
Those who always remember Īśāna or worship him, [attain liberation].
Having fallen from the world of Rudra, they are indeed Rudras; there is no doubt about this.
The Agnihotra rites, the Vedas, and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees—
even all these together— are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
He who always worships Śiva shall always perform sacrifice, always bestow gifts, and always subsist on air alone. (7.3)
To him who constantly worships Śiva or bows down with devotion,
Śiva, being pleased, bestows both yoga and liberation.
Whoever performs worship for a month, eating but one meal a day and with senses subdued,
does not obtain such a fruit even through all the great sacrifices.
Having always bathed the Liṅga on the full moon day, the new moon day, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Having fasted on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight for the sake of the Supreme Lord,
one should perform worship on the fourteenth day during both the morning and midday.
Having drunk the five products of the cow once, a man who eats sacrificial oblation while restraining his speech obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices. (7–8)
Having fasted on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and having worshipped Śaṅkara,
one attains the supreme abode of Maheśvara, the God of gods.
Having become pure and observing the vow of celibacy, one should worship Śiva during the twilight;
having delivered seven generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
One should worship Śiva on the festival days according to the procedure for the great ablution and other rites;
indeed, such worship of Śaṅkara should be performed at all times.
The merit that arises from worshipping on a festival day for such a duration is attained by worshipping with every effort, according to the extent of one's wealth.
Śiva should be worshipped constantly by one desiring to conquer the worlds of merit;
one should worship Śiva according to the prescribed rule without interruption for six months.
One obtains that very same merit through the worship performed at the equinox;
this indeed should be known to apply likewise during an eclipse and at the winter solstice.
On the transit of the sun, on the intercalary days, and on the days of the six-aśīti-mukha,
one obtains the merit gained by worshipping Śaṅkara according to the prescribed rite for four months.
The merit that comes from worshipping Śiva on the full moon day of Kārttika shall likewise be obtained on the full moon days of Phālguna and Āṣāḍha.
Indeed, this four-month worship yields the fruit of great merit;
he who is diligent in the month of Māgha should worship Śiva at the three junctions of the day.
One shall obtain the merit of six months in a single month; of this there is no doubt.
As it is in the month of Māgha, so it is in the month of Āṣāḍha and likewise in the month of Kārttika. (7.18)
The merit performed during these three months should be known as equal;
one obtains the merit of worshiping for four months by worshipping during the month of Puṣya.
The merit produced during the two months of Caitra and Phālguna, as well as the fortnightly merit on the fourteenth day, the new moon, and the full moon [is obtained]. (7.20)
The merit of one who worships Śiva on the eighth lunar day should be known as eightfold;
it is equal to that of one who gives a hundred thousand milch cows to a master of the Vedas.
The merit of one who worships the Liṅga for a single day is greater than that of the best of the twice-born who eats [only once] every month throughout his entire life.
And whoever worships the Liṅga even once, there is no doubt that through this sequential practice, there is an increase in merit day by day. (7.23)
Furthermore, he who, having abandoned attachment, worships the word "Śiva," [attains liberation].
His merit increases a hundredfold due to its continuity;
his merit is fiftyfold [when he worships] Śiva.
In every season it should be half of that, and even in a month it should be half of that;
he who worships [the Lord] in the linga continuously for even half a month— || 7.26 ||
Indeed, it is difficult for even the best of men to know the continuous [practice] of him who, having risen in the morning, worships the Liṅga even once with devotion. (7.27)
One shall obtain that fruit which is gained by giving away the entire earth;
when the sun has reached the meridian, one should worship continuously. (7.28) p. 80(106)
Whatever merit one might obtain by giving a hundred tawny cows,
that same merit he who properly worships Śiva obtains when the sun has entered the constellation Vāruṇī.
One shall obtain the fruit of giving away a hundred thousand cows;
for the Śiva-liṅga is of great merit and is saluted by all the gods.
Even he who merely touches them with his hands is not defiled by sins;
they shall no longer go to a womb within the ocean of saṃsāra.
Those men who attain liberation gradually by means of the mere linga—even a heap of sinful karma as vast as Mount Meru and Mandara—[will be purified]. (7.32)
Having approached the Lord, they are destroyed like malignant diseases;
one who is constantly devoted to the worship of the Liṅga is freed from the consequences of great sins. (7.33)
One would not be stained by the faults committed, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
even after cutting, piercing, and destroying all these living beings and this entire world.
One should worship the single Virūpākṣa; he is not defiled by sins, even if he has fallen into every condition or is joined with all manner of crimes.
Having worshipped Śiva, even that man goes to the supreme goal,
whether he is on the banks of rivers or oceans, or in forests and groves.
On mountain peaks, in wells, and in dense groves;
at lotus ponds, in reservoirs, and in the vicinity of holy fords and shrines.
Or wherever the intellect finds delight, there one should worship Śiva;
one will obtain the merit that comes from all forms of giving—of this there is no doubt. (7.38)
Furthermore, he who worships Śiva after having abandoned the formal resolve for ritual bathing obtains the entire fruit of a horse sacrifice; there is no doubt in this matter.
This heap of merit has been proclaimed even without a mantra;
when joined with a mantra, this merit becomes a hundred times greater. (7.40)
Therefore, with the mantra, one should offer bathing, perfumes, fruits, and so forth, as well as elephants, horses, chariots, garments, gold, and other such items for all [the deities]. (7.41)
First, the mantra "Namaḥ śivāya" accomplishes all aims;
this six-syllabled mantra, preceded by the syllable Om, is superior to all other mantras. (7.42)
All this world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded internally and externally by Śiva; because He created the universe as "Om," He is therefore designated by the name "Om. (7.43)
And this meaning is sung by means of three measures (mātrās); Brahmā, Hari, and Rudra are proclaimed as the three measures. (7.44)
The world is pervaded by these three causes, which are one's own actions;
these are the three measures (mātrās) of Śiva, honored by all the worlds.
These very [energies] are the three Vedas, the three worlds, the three fires,
the three qualities, the three aims of life, and whatever else exists in the world.
Beyond the half-mora is Rudra, Śiva, the supreme cause;
from him this triad of causes of the world has arisen.
The pure obeisance to Maheśvara is the fruit of all sacrifices;
therefore, one should worship Śiva with the sacrifice whose essence is obeisance. (7.48)
Ignorance is the Śiva-principle, since it is the abode of all suffering;
for Rudra, who is the Supreme Śiva, by his very nature, indeed removes that dust. (7.49)
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the cause of the three causes;
I offer myself unto you, O Supreme Lord, for you are my refuge.
By reciting "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," one is liberated from all sins;
therefore, one should always keep in mind this mantra beginning with the syllable Oṃ.
At all times and in all activities, even during such acts as eating or spitting,
he who proceeds toward Śiva after uttering the words "Obeisance to Śiva" (namaḥ śivāya) attains Śiva.
But he who is self-awakened and remembers [the mantra] when his life-breath departs—he who [utters] "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya"—shall go to the supreme goal. (7.53)
Even a prostration performed with deceit toward the wielder of the trident shall become the means of untying the coarse bonds of saṃsāra. (7.54)
Whether impure or pure, or even having reached any state whatsoever, he who remembers Rudra but once is liberated from all sins. (7.55)
Merely by the remembrance of Rudra, the cage of the multitude of sins shatters into a hundred pieces, just as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
For the accomplishment of all goals without exception for all devotees of Śiva, the mantra is Maheśvara himself, the direct means for accomplishing every purpose. (7.57)
That which is the seed of all sciences, the primordial Brahman, higher than the highest,
the mantra that accomplishes all aims— the six-syllabled Śivasūtra. (7-58)
From that very Sūtra spoken by Śambhu, the auspicious knowledges— both higher and lower— have been declared here in both explicit and implicit forms.
Therefore, one should perform the worship of Śiva with this mantra;
during the twilight (saṃdhyā), one should recite it for the purification of all sins.
A hundred times more merit than that is obtained from bathing in a body of water during the twilight;
however, at the southern face of Śiva (Dakṣiṇāmūrti), that merit is ten thousand times greater.
Therefore, for the sake of the perpetual accomplishment of all desires, one should constantly perform recitation (*japa*) with the mantra in the abode of Śiva.
For one who, with senses conquered and mind tranquil, worships with the Śiva-mantra,
his merit cannot be described even in hundreds of years.
This much can be said: even the land in which he dwells would become purified; how much more so his kinsmen? (7.64)
In whatever dwelling one eats, and whoever are one's attendants, they too should be known here as equal to that [deity]; without them, there is no worship of Śiva. (7.65)
In that land where Śaṅkara is worshipped, there shall be no famine nor shall plague prevail; the king does not die prematurely. (7.166)
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit that he obtains who, having been initiated and knowing the Sūtras and Mantras, worships Sadāśiva. (7.67)
Whatever merit is found in all the Vedas and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices—one obtains that fruit multiplied ten millionfold; of this there is no doubt. (7.68)
Whoever constantly worships Śiva—even if he be an outcaste—provided he has conquered his senses and is endowed with devotion to Bhava, he too shall attain the supreme goal. (7.69)
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) is superior to a thousand who have been initiated;
a student of the Vedas is superior to a thousand students of sacred knowledge.
One who maintains the sacred fire (agnihotrī) is indeed superior to thousands who merely study the Vedas;
one who performs sacrifices (yajñayājī) is superior to thousands who maintain the sacred fire.
One who performs a sacrificial session (sattra) is superior to thousands of performers of ordinary sacrifices;
those who have reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge are superior to thousands of performers of sacrificial sessions.
A devotee of Śiva excels even ten million experts in all branches of knowledge;
therefore, with a tranquil mind, one should worship Śiva. (7.73)
A devotee of Śiva who has conquered anger, who is devoted to the knowledge of Śiva, and who is constantly compassionate and friendly, attains eternal Śiva. (7.74)

Whatever merit one who is well-cultivated in loving-kindness (*maitrī*) might perform even for half a moment, that would not be attained even in a hundred years through asceticism or hundreds of sacrifices. (7.75)

One should cultivate compassion toward all living beings, and loving-kindness toward those who are miserable and protectorless; one should cultivate sympathetic joy toward those who possess merit and happiness. (7.76)
And equanimity toward those devoid of merit, as well as toward all others—having thus cultivated the mind in these five ways, one should worship Śiva. (7.77)
Having worshipped the Blessed Maheśvara with supreme devotion,
a person, having joined his palms in reverence, should recite this hymn of praise. (7.78)
Salutations to you, the three-eyed one, who are the form of praise for him who is praised, who are always being praised, and who are the repository of the causes of praise.
Salutation to you, the god of gods, the sole cause of all gods,
who is the illuminator even of those things that illuminate, the most radiant one.
Salutations to you, whose form is knowledge, the sole cause of all knowledge;
to you who are purified by knowledge and discernment, and who are eternally devoted to knowledge.
Salutations to You, the subtle one, subtler than the subtle, the sole cause of subtle knowledge, subtler even than the subtle, the most subtle of all.

Salutations to you, the divine one, who possesses a divine form, who is the sole cause of all divine forms, who is worthy of worship even by those who are themselves worthy of worship, and who are most worthy of honor.
Salutations to You, the eternally most eternal, the single cause of both the eternal and the non-eternal, and the eternal even among all things eternal. (7.84)
Homage to you, the blazing one, the most intensely blazing, the sole cause of all brilliance,
and the blazest even among those who blaze!
Salutations to You, the purest of the pure, who are pure, whose form is pure, the sole cause of all that is pure,
and who are the purity even of those who are pure.
Salutations to you, who are the essence, whose very form is the essence, the sole cause of all essences,
the essence even of essences, and the most excellent of all essences.
Salutations to You, the most powerful of all, who are Śakti itself, whose form is Śakti, the sole cause of all powers,
and who are the power even for those who possess power. (7.88)
Salutation to you, who are Time, who possess the form of Time, who are the sole cause of all time, and who are the Time even of times; salutation to you, the most profound darkness of Time.
Homage to you, whose body is all mantras, the sole cause of all mantras,
the mantra even among mantras, the supreme mantra!
Salutations again and again to Īśāna, whose form is the measure of space;
salutations again and again to Dharmeśa, whose nature is the measure of space. || 7-91 ||
Salutations again and again to the Lord of enjoyment, for the sake of enjoyment as vast as the sky;
salutations again and again to the Lord of liberation, for the sake of liberation as vast as the sky.
Salutations to you who possess one body, two bodies, and many bodies;
salutations again and again to Tryambaka, who is endowed with innumerable bodies.
Salutation to you who have one face, two faces, and many faces;
salutation to you, the Supreme Lord, endowed with innumerable faces.
Salutation to you who have one tongue, two tongues, and many tongues.
Salutations again and again to the one with countless tongues and three eyes.
Salutations to you who have one ear, two ears, and many ears;
salutations to you, the blue-throated one, endowed with innumerable ears.
Homage to you who have one nose, two noses, and many noses;
homage to you, Śarva, who are eternally endowed with various innumerable forms. || 7.97 ||
Homage to you who have one hand, two hands, or many hands;
homage again and again to Śaṅkara, who possesses innumerable hands. (7.98)
Salutations to you who are clad in one garment, two garments, and many garments;
salutations always to you, Rudra, who are endowed with innumerable garments.
Salutations to you who have one eye, two eyes, and many eyes;
salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, who is endowed with innumerable eyes.
Homage be to you, O Mahādeva; homage be to you, O Maheśvara! Homage to you, O Yogin; homage to you, O blazing one!
Homage be to you, the Great Lord; homage be to you, the Most Excellent One.
Homage be to you, O Great Form; homage be to you, Sadāśiva.
Salutations to you, O eternally pure one; salutations to you, [O * * * * *].
Salutations to you, O Mahādeva; [O * * Sadāśiva * *]. (7.103)
Salutations to you, O Blessed One, the Peaceful; salutations to you, O Blessed One, the Eternal;
salutations to you, O Blessed One, the Radiant; salutations to you, O Blessed One, the Destroyer.
Homage to you, the Unconquered; homage to you, whose limbs are smeared with ashes.
Homage to you, the All-Knowing; homage to you, the One Without Protector.
Salutations to you, the unmanifest; salutations be to you, the profoundly peaceful.
Salutations to you, the most worthy of worship; salutations be to you, the bestower of boons.
"Salutations to you, the infinite; salutations to you, the all-pervading.
He who praises Maheśvara with this divine hymn—
Having quickly shaken off all evils, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
one who desires enjoyments obtains enjoyments, and one who desires a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom. (7.108)
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease; the sufferer is liberated from suffering;
the bound is released from bondage; and one who seeks fame shall attain great renown. (7.109)
Having attained constant devotion to the Supreme Śiva, one’s happiness increases;
whatever desires a person contemplates, those very things he obtains. (7.110)
The man who constantly recites this attains the state of Śiva.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Rule for the Dharma of Giving," in the *Śivadharmaśāstra* spoken by the venerable Nandikeśvara.
Glorious One! Now begins the eighth chapter.
Nandikeśvara said:
Whatever sacred fords and meritorious shrines exist upon the earth, they all dissolve into the Liṅga; therefore, one should worship the Liṅga.
He who worships Mahādeva has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices; he shall go to the supreme state.
A *liṅga* installed by a hundred [people] should not be moved even by a thousand;
whether it be well-placed or poorly placed, one must never move a *śivaliṅga*.
He who, being diligent, performs the ghee-consecration (ghṛtābhiṣeka) of Śiva for a day and night with a vessel of fine spout during a meritorious month, [attains great merit]. || 8-4 ||
Performing the vigil there with offerings of song and dance, with the sounds of conchs and musical instruments, and with the splendor of lamps and other lights. (8.5)
Freed from all sins, joined with his entire lineage, his every desire fulfilled, and endowed with all virtues. || 8-6 ||
Endowed with blazing, equal, great vehicles—incalculable and incomparable—he rejoices eternally in the City of Śiva, happy like Śiva himself. (8-7)
Whoever performs an ablution with ghee during an eclipse, at the equinoxes, or on auspicious days, shall attain great merit.
He who, having fasted until its completion, witnesses the consecration with clarified butter (*ghṛtābhiṣeka*),
shakes off all sins and goes to the world of Śiva. (8–9)
One worships with devotion, while another perceives with devotion;
the fruit for both of them is exactly the same, for devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Whoever should undertake the performance of a great worship on the festival days of Śiva, or a chariot procession by circumambulating the interior of the city; || 8-11 ||
With great and variegated banners, adorned with colorful tinkling bells,
with canopies, rows of flags, bells, chowries, and mirrors.
With the resounding blasts of conchs, kettledrums, and the like, and amidst the clamor of songs and instrumental music,
[the deities] such as the hosts of Mothers and Yakṣas should be depicted by means of drawings or wooden mechanical figures.
It was adorned with many wonderful mechanical devices of the north and south,
such as triple-swinging wheels and chariot-palaces.
[He saw the city] provided with gardens, drinking saloons, and parks, endowed with great sacrificial sessions and assembly halls, crowded with many people, and arranged according to [his] wealth.
The merits of all forms of giving, the fruits of all sacrifices, the merit of those who perform most rigorous austerities, and the fruits of all sacred fords—[all these are attained]. (8.16)
Having obtained this, the illustrious one becomes free from disease; by initiating the ritual procession, he always rejoices like Śiva with great enjoyments in the world of Śiva.
At its conclusion, he shall attain the sovereignty of the king of gods for a very long time;
and at the end of that, he shall again become a glorious lord of Jambūdvīpa.
He who should offer a blanket of ghee as far as the edge of the altar on the full moon festival in the month of Māgha, his reward shall be equal to that of the continuous stream of ghee. (8.19)
Having performed the vigil with songs, dances, and other such acts even once on a festival day,
one is glorified in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred Manvantaras.
Having properly performed the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) of the delightful dance with parasols and other offerings before the temple of Śiva, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
One who is handsome, fortunate, and glorious is born here after falling [from a higher state].
Having fashioned an image made of flour with three eyes and adorned with jewels— || 8.22 ||
One should place pearls upon his teeth, coral upon his lower lips,
a diamond upon his eyes, and lapis lazuli upon his head.
One should fashion it of gold and silver with the two hands, or of copper for the feet;
one may also wrap it with eggs or with cotton threads.
One should adorn it with fragrant substances, incense, and flowers;
and there, one should prepare an offering (bali) consisting of various kinds of foods and edibles.
One should feed the devotees of Śiva and honor the Brahmins with devotion;
saying, "May Śiva be eternally pleased with me," one should dismiss the twice-born. (8-26)
Together with those very lords of brahmins, he should lead him to the temple of Śiva;
having led him there, he should place him upon the altar in the vicinity of the Śiva-liṅga.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices and the fruits of all gifts, one who gives land is honored in the world of Śiva by means of that gift of land. || 8-28 ||
One should give a vessel filled with ghee and adorned with honey, along with one *māgadha-prastha* of black sesame seeds. (8.29)
One should prepare a separate prastha of double the amount of rice,
wrapped in variegated cloths from Aṇḍaja and Pauṇṭra.
Having wrapped the linga with two garments, one should present this bali offering,
especially on the full moon day, after having worshipped according to the prescribed rule.
He is glorified in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions of yugas;
when his merit is exhausted, he returns here and is born into a prosperous family.
He shall be intelligent, fortunate, illustrious, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
having filled a copper vessel with milk and placed gold within it— (8.33)
Having covered [the vessel] with a lotus on top...
having honored the twice-born devotee of Śiva according to the prescribed rite.
When the moon has arisen in the east and the sun has moved to the west,
on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha, one should place the domestic vessel before Śiva.
"May Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, whose form is Soma, be pleased with me.
With devotion, he should slowly offer that vessel to that Brahmin. (8.36)
Having performed this vow called Saumavrata, one should go to the presence of Rudra;
fallen from the world of Rudra, that man shall become a rememberer of his past births.
He shall not return again to the state of Śiva merely through previous practice;
rather, having diligently worshipped Śiva on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, [he attains it]. || 8-38 ||
One should offer a sacred thread to Śiva and feed those who are devotees of Śiva;
then again, on the full moon day of Kārttika, having worshipped Śambhu, one should ask for his forgiveness.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the ascetics, preceded by [gifts of] sacred threads, garments, and so forth;
whoever performs the Cāturmāsya-pavitraka rite even once in this manner, [attains the fruit]. (8.40)
For a hundred divine crores of kalpas he is honored in the world of Rudra;
when his merit is exhausted and he has fallen from there, he is born as one who knows the four Vedas.
By his own will, he may become a king endowed with virtue and beauty;
[he obtains] whatever merit belongs to the gift of land and whatever fruit belongs to the gift of a daughter. (8.42)
Whatever merit a person obtains through instrumental music, that same merit is obtained through song and especially through dance. (8.43)
That indeed is the merit of the word "Victory" (jaya), and that is the merit of the sound of the conch;
he who would give a milch cow, young and accompanied by a bull, [attains that same merit].
By him it was given for the sake of Śiva; thus the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, would have been given.
It was the noble bull, with its limbs complete, possessing the luster of the moon. (8.45)
One should also offer a bull, a beast of burden, and whatever else is desired; as many as are the hairs on its body and those born in its lineage, [so many sins are destroyed]. (8.46)
For as many thousands of yugas as there are cows of beautiful form and excellent milk given for the purpose of the Śiva-fire-rite, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
By giving a noble tawny cow, one's gift becomes inexhaustible;
the tawny cow protects [her giver] like a mother from fears, wildernesses, and difficult passes. (8.48)
Therefore, one should offer the *kapilā* cow during the sacrifice to Śiva;
for the purpose of Śiva’s bathing and other rites, *kapilā* ghee has been produced. (8.49)
Therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should employ that very [practice] there; for if a Śūdra, devoid of the Śiva-consecration, should drink the Kāpila [milk], [it would be disastrous]. (8.50)
He goes to a most terrible hell filled with agonies;
a Brahmin should drink what remains after the oblation has been offered, for otherwise he would be like a beast. (8.51)
Having touched a cow and paid homage, he who performs two circumambulations has,
by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
Since sin is destroyed by the sound of the cows' "hum" and by seeing or touching them, one should always look upon them and touch them. (8.53)
How indeed could there be sins for those whose houses are adorned with cows that are constantly accompanied by their young calves, as if they were the goddesses Śrī herself?
Whatever holy places there are on earth up to the ocean, and whatever lakes—
by bathing in the water from a cow's horn, they do not equal even a sixteenth part [of its merit].
One should not leap over the bones of a cow, and one should avoid the smell of the dead;
for as long as one smells that odor, for that long one is filled with merit.
By scratching the cows, by offering incense, and by protecting them from fear, disease, and other harms, one obtains a fruit equal to the gift of a hundred cows. || 8.57 ||
He who provides grass, water, and other necessities near cows obtains the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. (8.58)
What is the use of saying more here? Cows must be protected with great effort;
cows are gods who must always be guarded, nourished, and protected at all times. (8.59)
Those wicked ones who strike the cow, the mother of all the world, and those who revile her—by them the entire world is reviled and struck. (8.60)
If that lowest of men should strike a cow out of delusion,
he shall be cooked in the fire of hell, oppressed by the cows' own sighs, for as long as he cries out.
He should turn them back by striking them with a staff of *palāśa* wood;
he should say to them, "Go! Go! and restrain them by saying, "Mother! Mother! (62).
One who should perform the ritual release of the bull on either of the two fortnights, on the twelfth day, or on the full moon, or on the fourteenth or eighth days; || 8.63 ||
May Viṣṇu, who is fond of his devotees, Śiva, Umā, and all the deities, being pleased, nourish my peace, heaven, longevity, strength, and prosperity. (8.64)
Thus, one who behaves toward cows with kindness, avoiding beating and abuse, attains great prosperity and goes to the world of Rudra. || 8-68 ||
If one who is striving for the sake of cows and Brahmins should even be deprived of life,
he attains the supreme abode where the Lord Maheśvara dwells.
The lineage of Brahmins and that of cows are indeed one and the same, though divided into two; in one part reside the mantras, and in the other resides the sacrificial oblation.
In cows the sacrifices proceed; in cows the gods are established;
by cows the Vedas are pervaded, together with their six ancillaries, word-for-word analyses, and phonetic recitations.
At the base of the horns of cows, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally present;
at the tips of the horns are all sacred fords, both stationary and moving. (8.69)
Mahādeva is situated in the center of the head, standing above all the gods;
the Goddess is stationed at the tip of the forehead, and Ṣaṇmukha is on the bridge of the nose.
The two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara, are stationed in the nostrils;
the two divine Aśvins are in the ears; and the Moon and the Sun are in the eyes.
All the Vasus reside in the teeth; Varuṇa is situated in the tongue;
Sarasvatī is in the syllable "huṃ"; and Yama and Yakṣa are in the two cheeks.
Likewise, at the two junctures [of day and night], Indra has taken refuge in the neck by means of the two lips;
the constellations and the heavens are in the hump, and the Siddhas are situated upon the chest.
The entire Dharma stands itself as the four legs, positioned upon the shanks;
within the hooves are the Gandharvas, and at the tips of the hooves are the Pannagas.
The hosts of Apsarases reside at the tips of the hooves;
the eleven Rudras are on the back, and the Vāyus are in all the joints.
The Pitṛs reside in the hips, while the Mātṛs are situated in the womb;
Śrī is always present in the drinking vessel of cows, and the Nāgas take refuge in the tail.
The rays of the sun are established as if condensed into a mass within his hair;
the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, is contained within his belly. (8.77)
The Gaṅgā is present directly in the cow's urine, and the Yamunā resides in the cow dung;
twenty-eight crores of gods are well-established within the pores of his skin.
Likewise, all the sages are situated within the pores of her skin;
the four oceans are full, like the udders of a cow. (8.79)
The Gārhapatya fire is in the belly, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is in the heart, and the Āhavanīya fire is indeed in the mouth; thus they abide within that most venerable [body].
All sacrifices, such as the horse sacrifice and others, reside within the joints [of the body].
Indeed, all this has been explained just as it is established in the cows.
In cows, everything that is given, offered in sacrifice, or consumed—including all that is moving and unmoving—is contained.
Therefore, one must certainly not harm cows; they should always be protected.
Cows are to be praised and cows are to be revered; may cows protect me eternally.
That Brahmin who is praised by the word "Brahman" through the syllable Om— || 8.83 ||
May that eternal god Śiva, who is accompanied by Ambā and honored by Vighneśa and the Gaṇas, dispel all calamities for cows both in this world and the next.
May that eternal god Śiva dispel the plagues among the cattle—
he who was praised by the elephant-faced god Lambodara.
May that eternal god Śiva dispel the plagues among cattle—
he who [is served] by the illustrious Rucirnāga and the Gaṇa Ghaṇṭākarṇa.
May the eternal God Śiva, who is perpetually saluted with devotion by one whose mind is never forsaken [by Him] and who is filled with joy, dispel all calamities from the cattle. (8.87)
Constantly endowed with the power of Rudra and possessed of Rudra’s energy,
the divine Ghaṇṭākarṇa is a leader of the Gaṇas who carries out the commands of Śiva.
May Śiva, through the power of his splendor, dispel all diseases among the cattle—
for the sake of the auspicious one, the God of gods, the Great God, the radiant one. (8.89)
Salutations again and again to Rudra, the Immovable One, who is eternally free from disease;
to the Supreme Lord, the Perfected One, the bestower of the attainment of mantras.
"Salutation to you, the three-eyed Maheśa, who are exceedingly peaceful";
having consecrated the water constantly with these mantras in their proper order— || 8-91 ||
One should sprinkle water on the bodies of cows; thus, peace will prevail.
He who recites this, especially when cows are afflicted by disease, [shall obtain great merit].
One should always recite the Go-sāvitrī; thus there will be peace for cows.
Rising early in the morning, one should constantly recite this Go-sāvitrī.
At the times of the cows' departure or their gathering, one shall become long-lived, strong, glorious, possessed of cattle, and a lord of wealth. (8-94)
And at the end of the body, one shall go to the supreme abode; there is no doubt in this matter.
For the sake of purification from all sins, one should recite this *gosāvitrī*.
May the cows, together with their bulls and healthy calves, graze happily in the forests upon waters and lush grasses.
May they provide milk; may they sleep in peace.
Having adorned an excellent horse and offered it to Śivā,
one shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One should offer a well-disciplined woman, a female slave, or a servant;
the fruit of this shall be eightfold that of the human sacrifice (naramedha). || 8.98 ||
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who, with devotion, offers a well-adorned auspicious elephant to Śiva on a festival day. (8–99)
He sports with hundreds of magnificent great vehicles, yoked to many intoxicated elephants resembling Airāvata. || 8.100 ||
For thousands of millions of kalpas and tens of millions of ayutas of kalpas,
he shall go to the world of Rudra, and at the end, he shall become Indra, the lord of the gods.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, having attained the earth,
that lord of men shall become equal to Indra, glorious and endowed with beauty, heroism, and majesty.
Listen to the fruit of merit for that lord of the earth who, for the sake of Śiva, gives land endowed with fruits and causing all crops to grow. (8.103)
As many daṇḍas as there would be of earth when measured all around,
for that many kalpas he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
In this manner, the result should be understood everywhere according to the measure of the staff, in the reporting of villages, hamlets, cities, fields, districts, and so forth. (8.105)
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who gives a village endowed with all crops and water, and free from all afflictions, to Śiva. (8.106)
Whatever merit is found in all sacrifices, whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords,
and whatever merit is found in all acts of giving— that same fruit is obtained by the gift of a village.
Resplendent like ten million suns, accompanied by ten million divine women,
he is joined by many millions and endowed with all objects of desire. (8.108)
By the gift of a village together with its three surrounding settlements,
one dwells for an inexhaustible time, sporting as one desires in the world of Īśvara, accompanied by twenty-one generations of one's family.
The merit from giving a village is more than a hundredfold that of a city;
and the infinity resulting from the gift of ten [villages] cannot be fully described.
Jewels, food, drink, cattle, horses, and other such things arise for one who rules as a sovereign;
therefore, by the gift of land, a man becomes [prosperous] at all times.
That lowest of men who seizes land given by another or given by himself shall be cooked in the hells for an inexhaustible period of time, one after another. (8.112)
In the seizure of land, everything is indeed taken; of this there is no doubt.
The seizer of land shall dwell in that hell for an inexhaustible period of time.
Men who misappropriate the property of the gods here, being fearless of hell,
and those who, out of delusion, seize the property of Brahmins, are cooked in the fires of hell.
The mounts nourished by the property of gods and Brahmins crumble for the lord of the earth at the time of battle, like embankments made of sand.
For as many years as the donor shall dwell in heaven, the number of those years is said to be multiplied by a hundred for the one who steals it; he shall dwell in hell.
Indeed, there are twenty-eight most dreadful hells;
those who steal the property of gods or Brahmins are cooked within them in succession.
At the end of the eon, they have emerged from births as insects in trees and the like; tormented by hunger, thirst, and other such afflictions, they wander for a very long time. (8.118)
Thus they wander for a very long time, impelled by the command of Īśvara, until [they are led] by some devotee of Śiva to the temples and other sites of Śiva’s worship. (8.119)
Then, their sins shaken off by the power of Śiva,
those men cast off their bodies produced by torment and proceed to the divine realm.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of the Śiva-dharma," in the Śiva-dharmottara, a Śaiva scripture proclaimed by Nandikeśvara.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Nandikeśvara said: O best of sages, hereafter I shall declare this secret, which is endowed with supreme merit and practiced by all the gods. (9.1)
By Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Goddess, Skanda, Indra, and Yama;
and by Varuṇa, Āditya, Soma, Agni, Marut, Hanumān, and Nārada. || 9-2 ||
By Dharmaśrī, Śukra, the lunar mansion, Vilohita, Śanaiścara,
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Bṛhaspati, Budha, and the others.
[He was attended] by Śveta, Agastya, Dadhīca, and all the other most excellent sages,
as well as by Bhṛṅgin, Mātṛ, Mahākāla, Caṇḍeśvara, and the Lord of the Gaṇas.
By Vṛṣa, Vāsuki, Kārkoṭaka, Gulika, Ananta,
Takṣaka, Śaṅkha, Padma, Mahāpadma, and other great serpents as well.
By many Siddhas, Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and high-souled beings;
and also by Apsarases, Daityas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and hosts of Bhūtas.
Just as the path to Śiva was attained by all the Viśvedevas and by those various excellent performers of meritorious deeds—a path that surpasses all other states of existence. (9.7)
Listen to how this occurred through the grace of Īśa:
having bathed the liṅga with water scented with white sandalwood and having smeared it [with unguents]. (9.8)
Having worshipped and prostrated with hundreds of blooming lotuses— pure, gentle, flawless, flowering, and white— upon that stainless and auspicious lotus, [he spoke]. (9-9)
Having placed the smallest liṅga, auspicious and composed of all fragrances, measuring the size of a thumb, according to the rules in the middle of the cluster of filaments; 9-10.
Having established [the deity] in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should worship with bilva leaves;
agaru (sandalwood) on the right side, and red arsenic (manaśśilā) on the west.
One should offer sandalwood in the north and yellow orpiment in the east;
one should also worship with very fragrant and variegated flowers. || 9-12 ||
One should offer black aloe-wood incense as well as guggulu mixed with clarified butter;
one should present garments that are clean, fine, and free of loose threads.
Taking refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti with the auspicious mantra for the sake of Śiva,
all the gods attained divinity by means of this ritual procedure.
The Goddess attained the state of Devī; Guha attained the state of Skanda;
Brahmā attained the state of Brahman; and Hari attained the state of Viṣṇu. (9.15)
Indra attained the sovereignty over the gods, and the Gaṇas attained the status of Gaṇas;
thus, he who worships the Liṅga composed of all fragrances even once [attains these]. (9.16)
Freed from all sins, one attains Śiva alone;
this supreme vow is secret, the great vow of the Śiva-liṅga. (9.17)
This has been declared by me to you, my devotee; it must not be given to just anyone.
He who removes a garland that has long been worn by Śiva— || 9.18 ||
There is no doubt that for him there arises the fruit of a thousand cows.
Thus ends the "Great Vow of the Śiva-liṅga" in the *Śivadharmottara*, a treatise on the *Śivadharma*.
The Ninth Chapter.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Nandikeśvara,
being pure and devoted to the worship of Śiva, should not eat for one year on the fourteenth and eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights.

Whatever inexhaustible merit is said to belong to those who constantly perform sacrificial sessions (sattra), whatever merit belongs to speakers of truth, and whatever merit belongs to those who visit sacred fords (tīrtha); ||| 10-2 ||
Whatever merit lies in the Agnihotra sacrifices and whatever merit belongs to those who perform Vedic sacrifices—
all that merit he obtains in its entirety, and he goes to the world of Śiva.
Having used the earth as a vessel and eaten with great care from leaves,
one enjoys the fruit of a three-night fast by means of a single day and night.
On the two fifth days of the lunar fortnights and on the two first days, a man,
having observed a fast and having anointed his body with fragrant scents, should lie down with his beloved.
He lies with a motionless mind, devoid of passion and attachment;
hear now the fruit of the merit belonging to him whose mind is fixed on the recollection of Śiva. || 10-6 ||
For a thousand divine years and a hundred divine years, great austerity was performed by him; of this there is no doubt. (10.7)
Even if he be a doer of evil, one whose soul is thoroughly purified by devotion to Śiva shall dwell eternally in the world of Śiva, being remembered as equal to Śiva in his virtues. (10.8)
By eating only at night from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one attains enjoyments in this world and a blissful state in the hereafter. (10.9)
For one year, he should perform the *nakta* rite on every lunar festival (*parvan*),
remaining celibate, having conquered anger, and intent upon the worship of Śiva.
At the end of the year, having fed the foremost of Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva with concentrated devotion, he should then say: "May the Blessed Lord Śiva be pleased."
Thus, endowed with this ritual procedure, he goes to the world of Śiva;
he shall not return to the unstable world of mortals.
Alms-gathering is superior to fasting; not asking for alms is superior to begging; eating at night is superior to not asking; therefore, there is nothing superior to eating at night.
The gods eat in the forenoon, likewise the sages at midday,
the ascetics in the afternoon, and the Guhyakas and others at twilight.
Transcending all other times, the eating at night is supreme;
Mahādeva, who follows the left-hand path (vāmācāra), delivers men by means of the nocturnal meal.

One should practice eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), remaining in a fixed posture, truthfulness, moderation in food, performing fire rituals, attending upon the sacred fires, and eating only at night. || 10.16 ||
Having diligently fashioned an Ananta image according to the prescribed rite on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
one should worship Śaṅkara in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having drunk cow's urine according to one's capacity, one should worship at night while abstaining from food;
the fruit of this shall be eightfold that of the Atirātra sacrifice.
