Likewise, having worshipped the Lord named Śambhu under the Puṣya asterism,
and consuming clarified butter on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one obtains the merit of eight Vājapeya sacrifices. (10.19)
In the month of Māgha, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the deity named Māheśvara;
by drinking cow’s milk at night, one obtains the merit of eight horse-sacrifices.
And in the month of Phālguna, having worshipped Mahādeva, one should consume sesame seeds;
one shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
For a hundred thousand years, he is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments;
one should worship the one named Sthāṇu on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra.
Having consumed as much as can be comfortably swallowed, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
in the month of Vaiśākha, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass at night while reciting the name of Śiva.
One shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the human-sacrifice (naramedha). Having worshipped Paśupati in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should drink water from the horns of cows.
One shall obtain that fruit which results from the gift of ten million cows,
having worshipped the one named Ugra in the month of Āṣāḍha and having consumed cow-dung.
One shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice; in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should eat oil-cake while observing the vow named after Śarva.
For more than a full hundred million years, one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Tryambaka.
By consuming bilva leaves, one obtains infinite fruit;
and by drinking rice-water from the one named Āśvijeśvara, one indeed attains the same.
The fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice shall be eightfold;
having worshipped the one named Rudra in the month of Kārttika, one should consume curd. (10.29)
One shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
at the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva.
One should devotedly offer them milk-rice mixed with honey and saturated with ghee, along with gold and garments according to one's ability. (10.31)
That man who performs this for the god continuously for one year should offer a black, milch cow to Rudra.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of his who observes the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow with devotion:
he shall be completely liberated from all sins and endowed with all forms of sovereignty. (10.33)
He shall dwell eternally in the city of Śiva and never return here again,
even during all meritorious festivals, at Viṣṇu’s appearances, or during eclipses and other such occasions.
Whatever is performed—such as giving, fasting, and fire-offerings—becomes inexhaustible.
I shall now describe this unsurpassed vow for each month. (10.35)

For the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, whoever should observe the practice of eating only at night during the months of Puṣya for embodied beings such as men and women, [attains these goals]. (10.36)
Truthful in speech and having conquered anger, he should diligently observe a fast on the eighth day of both fortnights, subsisting on rice, wheat, and dairy products.

One should worship the Lord at the three junctions of the day and perform fire-rituals according to one's ability; furthermore, at the end of the month on the full moon, one should sleep on the ground and offer unbroken rice grains and other oblations.
Having performed his bath and a great worship, he should diligently offer oblations to Śiva;
he should present as an offering one *āḍhaka* or *prastha* of milk-mixed parched grain (*kṣīrasakta*). || 10.39 ||
One should feed eight Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva with excellent sacrificial fees;
he who offers a pair of cattle and a tawny cow to Śiva [attains the same merit]. || 10.40 ||
Listen to the fruit of his merit after he has adorned his own form:
[he shall travel] in celestial chariots that shine like ten million suns and grant all desires.
[The mountain] was crowded with Rudra-maidens, joined by great bulls,
adorned by throngs of Apsarases, and graced with song, dance, instrumental music, and the like.
Fanned by chowries and praised by gods and asuras,
he was three-eyed, wielder of the trident, and endowed with the sovereignty of Śiva.
One shall go to that city of Śiva where Śaṅkara himself resides;
and for as many hairs as there are on his body, so many [members] shall be liberated in the families of those who gave birth to him.
For that many thousands of years, he is glorified in the world of Śiva,
having enjoyed desired pleasures together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Having attained the yoga of knowledge, one is liberated right there on this earth;
through yoga one reaches the end of suffering, and from knowledge yoga proceeds. (10.46)
Knowledge arises from the Śiva-dharma, and the Śiva-dharma arises from the worship of Śiva;
thus has this been fully explained for those wandering in the ocean of saṃsāra. (10.47)

For those who resort to and serve Śiva as the means for the gradual attainment of liberation, if one should observe the practice of eating only at night when the month of Māgha has arrived, [he attains that goal]. (10.48)
One who has restrained the senses, while eating kṛsara mixed with ghee,
should observe a fast on the fourteenth day of both fortnights. (10.49)
On the full moon day, he who would offer a ghee-blanket to Śiva should also present here a pair of black cows of beautiful form.
Having performed the remainder according to the rule, one shall obtain everything previously described;
[one shall travel] in celestial chariots resembling sapphire, surrounded by peacocks.
Having gone to the beautiful city of Śiva and having enjoyed pleasures as desired,
he who observes the practice of eating only at night when the month of Phālguna has arrived— || 10.52 ||
With his anger dispelled and his senses conquered, he should devote himself to fasting on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, subsisting on śyāmāka grain, milk, and nīvāra rice.
On the full moon day, one should perform the great ablution with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), ghee, and so forth;
likewise, with the barks of milk-exuding trees and fragrant substances such as *dhātrī*.
With devotion, one should offer a pair of copper-colored cows to the Supreme Lord (*Parameṣṭhin*).
Having performed the remaining rites as prescribed, one attains that fruit by means of celestial chariots resembling rubies and accompanied by elephants. (10.56)
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva as previously described, he obtains the fruit;
this applies to one who observes the practice of eating only at night when the month of Caitra has arrived.
Eating rice mixed with milk while his senses are restrained,
he should give there a pair of tawny cows (a *gomithuna*), well-adorned and accompanied by a *pāṭala* flower.
He attains the true nature of Śiva, and he should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
[He travels] on vehicles resembling rubies, yoked with divine horses and chariots. (10.59)

He who, when the month of Vaiśākha has arrived, observes the practice of eating only at night, shall go to the beautiful city of Śiva, which is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined themselves.
Eating flour-cakes mixed with milk while his senses are restrained, sleeping in a cow-pen, meditating on Śiva, and wearing a single garment during the night; 10.61.
One should perform all the general observances as prescribed;
and on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should perform a ritual bath with ghee and other substances.
One should offer to Śiva a white pair of cows, auspiciously adorned;
they shall be adorned with great celestial vehicles possessing the luster of swans, jasmine, and the moon.
Yoked with very white bulls, he proceeds to the abode of Īśvara,
surrounded by women whose forms surpass all others.
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night shall sport for an inexhaustible time with women fragrant as blue lotuses. (10.65)
Eating rice washed with water and combined with ghee and milk,
one who observes the vīrāsana posture for half the night shall follow the gods during the day.
Always acting for the benefit of cows and free from egoism,
he should perform the ritual procedures beginning with the bath on the day before the full moon.
In this rite, a pair of cows, smoke-colored and adorned, should be given away—
cows that are peerless and beyond counting, resembling the petals of the blue lotus.
And he plays for an inexhaustible time with those bound upon great lion-thrones;
this is for one who, when the month of Āṣāḍha has arrived, observes the practice of eating only at night. (10.69)
One should offer a mixture of many pieces of sugar-candy, parched grain flour, liquor, and milk;
and one should present to Śiva a pair of white cows, auspiciously adorned.
One should perform the general ritual procedure and everything previously enjoined,
[visualizing them] with vehicles resembling pure crystal and drawn by swans.
Endowed with the qualities of *aṇimā* and the rest, he shall move about by himself like Śiva;
so it is for one who observes the practice of eating only at night when the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived. (10.72)
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, one should offer a pair of white cows with pale-colored hooves and horns, accompanied by milk and *śāṣṭika* rice, to Śiva.
One should perform the entire common rite as it has been proclaimed by the ritual injunction, [providing] various great vehicles yoked with diverse horses. || 10.74 ||
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva as previously described, he obtains that fruit;
so it is for one who observes the practice of eating only at night when the month of Bhādrapada has arrived.
Eating only the remnants of the oblation, dwelling at the foot of a tree during the day,
and residing in a sanctuary at night, he should be compassionate toward all living beings.
One should offer to Rudra a bull with a blue hump and a cow,
adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli that shine like the rays of the moon.
Having traveled in celestial chariots that go everywhere and are adorned with ruddy geese,
they go to the delightful city of Śiva, which is worshipped by gods and asuras.
He who observes the practice of eating only at night during the glorious month of Āśvayuja shall sport with various enjoyments until the dissolution of all beings. (10.79) p. 113(139)
One who is serene in soul and has conquered the senses should employ the consumption of ghee;
[one should visualize] a bull with the luster of a dark-blue color, its chest region well-developed. (10.80)
Having released [the victim], one should give a single cow, well-adorned, to Rudra;
and one should perform the remainder of the ritual procedure in its entirety, as previously described.
At the end of his life, the self-controlled one goes to the supreme abode like Śiva,
[seated] upon [a throne] resembling clear pearls and adorned with sapphires.
Accompanied by *jīvañjīvaka* birds, he sports in celestial chariots that travel everywhere,
enjoying great pleasures until the dissolution of all beings.
In the auspicious month of Kārttika, he who observes the practice of eating only at night—truthful in speech and with senses subdued—should eat rice mixed with milk. (10.84)
In this rite, one should give a pair of Kapila cows with the brilliance of fire;
having performed it according to the previously mentioned procedure, one becomes equal in qualities to Śiva.
In a state of bliss, he acts like Śiva, seated upon great vehicles resembling the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon, incomparable and displaying the majestic stride of a great lion.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he who observes the practice of eating only at night, consuming barley-meal mixed with milk while his senses are restrained; || 10-87 ||
One should give a divine pair of white cows, well-adorned;
the remainder of the rite should be undertaken for Śiva according to the previously mentioned procedure.
By means of vehicles resembling white lotuses and yoked with white horses,
having gone to the divine city of Śiva, one shall become equal in power to Śiva. (10.89)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, forbearance, compassion, bathing three times a day, worship, fire-offerings, lying on the ground, and eating only at night. || 10.90 ||
By fasting on the two fortnights and on the fourteenth and eighth days,
and by such rules as these, one should observe the Śiva-vrata.
A woman who is a devotee of Śiva will certainly become a man;
she desires that most excellent state of womanhood—listen now to her vow.
This [teaching] named Umāmaheśvara increases eternal joy;
it brings about supreme yoga, is peaceful, and is the means for accomplishing dharma, desire, and wealth. (10.93)

On the full moon day, the new moon day, and on the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, she should observe the *nakta* fast for a year, eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) while remaining celibate (*brahmacāriṇī*).
Having fashioned a very beautiful image named Umāmaheśvara out of gold,
and having bathed it with ghee and other substances at the end of the year, || 10.95 ||
Having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, as well as beautiful cloth-flowers,
and with all kinds of food— both solid and soft— together with canopies, banners, and chowries.
One should feed the devotees of Śiva and satisfy the poor and the helpless;
and according to one's ability, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru who has bestowed the knowledge.
Having prepared a vessel made of gold, bell-metal, or other materials, and having smeared it with white ashes, one should place the image in the center of the sanctuary.
Carrying that vessel upon his head, adorned with canopies and parasols, and accompanied by the splendor of banners, conchs, and other regalia, he should lead it to the temple of Śiva. (10.99)
At the conclusion of the vow dedicated to Maheśa in his linga-form, one should offer [the gift];
one should place that vessel, adorned with ornaments, upon the altar.
Having circumambulated Śiva and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness;
having completed that meritorious vow, one should hear [the account] and obtain the fruit.
In a world of sovereign power, he rejoices together with the Rudras upon incomparable Great Vehicles that resemble twelve suns, according to his desire.
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
at the end of that time, he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu along with great enjoyments.
Then, by the remainder of his karma, having reached the world of Brahmā which is endowed with all objects of desire, he shall attain supreme happiness.
Fallen from the world of Brahmā, she was Śrīmatī, who was fully honored;
having attained the realm of Prajāpati, she was saluted by the worlds and the Lokālokas.
Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time, he shall dwell happily in the world of Soma;
from the world of Soma, having reached the supreme world of Indra, he shall become the lord of Indra.
Having departed from the world of Indra and reached the world of the Gandharvas, he rejoices;
having enjoyed all desired pleasures, he attains the status of a lord of the Gandharvas.
Having reached this world of the yakṣas, which is adorned with wonderful splendors shining with the light of great jewels, one rejoices according to one's desire.
Falling from the world of the yakṣas, the celestial Arundhatī sports;
having successively attained the stations of the world-protectors, she rejoices. (10.109)
At the edge of the world and throughout the entire circle of the earth,
wherever it may be, he shall obtain every divine happiness in its entirety.
Having obtained this one who is endowed with youth and beauty, who is the lord of the entire earth,
and who knows the dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, she rejoices.
Then, by virtue of the remainder of that merit, she becomes imbued with lordship;
through the application of the cultivation of her own karma, she again undertakes what is auspicious.
Or again, whether auspicious or otherwise, one wanders through thousands of such births by the power of karma as long as one does not attain world-weariness.
From that disillusionment comes detachment; from detachment arises knowledge;
from knowledge yoga proceeds; and from yoga one attains the end of suffering.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, she should remain strictly celibate and eat only once a day for one year, desiring to attain great enjoyments.
At the end of the year, having fashioned an image, one should perform the ritual as previously prescribed;
having completed the vow beginning and ending with the ceremonial bath, one shall obtain the aforementioned qualities.
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva by means of vehicles made of Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with four gates, one shall obtain every enjoyment in its entirety.
For the sake of her beloved, Queen Umā, having observed the fourteenth-day fast for a year, praised [him] according to the ultimate truth. (10.118)
At the end of the rainy season, having fashioned an auspicious image made of rice flour,
one should worship it with yellow ointments, garlands, and yellow garments. (10.119)
Having performed everything previously described, one should offer it to Śiva;
[the donor shall travel] in great seven-storied celestial vehicles with the luster of molten gold.
For the duration of many thousands of millions of yugas, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
having enjoyed all desired pleasures in Śiva’s world and every other world, [he eventually attains liberation].
Having come in due course to this world, she shall obtain a husband according to her desire;
she should remain thus well-restrained, fasting on the new moon day.
Having fashioned a trident out of flour, one should offer it at the end of the year;
and to Śiva, a silver lotus with a pericarp made of gold.
Out of devotion to Him, one should place [the mantra] upon the head; the remainder should be performed as before.
Whatever sin has been committed even through desire, such as the killing of an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā) and so forth—
A woman shall undoubtedly shatter all that by the gift of a trident,
[seated] upon a great lotus-palatial chariot accompanied by men and women.
For more than a full hundred crores of yugas, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
having enjoyed manifold pleasures in the worlds beginning with the realm of Īśa, he dwells there.
In this world, having attained [her desires] in due order, she shall obtain a husband according to her wish,
provided she remains well-restrained for one year on the full moon and new moon days.
At the end of the year, one should present an image enriched with all kinds of perfumes, [mounted] upon most wonderful great vehicles adorned with divine gandharvas. (10.128)
For more than a full hundred crores of yugas, he is honored in the world of Śiva;
having especially enjoyed pleasures at will in the world of Īśvara. (10.129)
Having come in due course to this world, she shall obtain a king as her husband—
she who subsists on a single meal during the auspicious month of Kārttika.
Endowed with the observances of forbearance, non-violence, and so forth, and remaining celibate,
she should offer oil-cake mixed with molasses and clarified butter at the end of the month.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, one should be devoted to fasting;
[thereby, one travels] by means of all-pervading celestial chariots resembling sapphire.
For more than a full hundred million years, he is honored in the world of Rudra,
having enjoyed manifold pleasures in the worlds beginning with that of Īśa.
Having obtained enjoyments according to her merit, especially in the various worlds,
she shall eventually come to this world and obtain a husband as she desires.
Thus, the rule for all months is proclaimed to be the same;
the wise know that the fruit of eating once [a day] and fasting are equal.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses, worship of Śiva, fire-offerings, contentment, and the cultivation of non-stealing. (10.136)
Whatever dharma is common to all vows has been remembered as being tenfold; I shall now also explain the specific [dharma] pertaining to each monthly vow.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having adorned a bull well-fashioned from flour with perfumes and garlands, one should offer it to Śiva.
In great vehicles yoked with bulls and accompanied by hosts of apsarases,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand years. (10.139)
Having attained supreme happiness among all the hosts of gods,
she shall gradually return to this world and obtain a husband according to her desire.
When the auspicious month of Puṣya has arrived, having fashioned a trident for the wielder of the Pināka bow,
one should adorn it with perfumes and garlands and offer it to Śiva.
By means of the great Puṣpaka vehicle, possessing divine fragrance and radiance,
one is honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred thousand divine years.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures arising from all cities,
and having attained the worlds in due order, she shall obtain a husband according to her desire.

In the month of Māgha, having fashioned a chariot yoked with horses, beautifully adorned with garlands of lamps, and equipped with a liṅga made of flour, one should bring it to the sacrificial ground.
By means of vehicles resembling great chariots, adorned with white horses,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of years.
Having experienced incomparable enjoyments arising from all cities,
she will gradually return to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
In the month of Phālguna, having fashioned an image made of flour and endowed with beauty,
and having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should place it in the presence of Śiva.
He is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand years by means of incomparable divine vehicles filled with songs and instrumental music.
Having attained supreme happiness among all the hosts of immortals,
she shall gradually return to this world and obtain a husband according to her desire. (10.149)
Having fashioned an image of the Youth (Kumāra) out of flour and adorned it in the month of Caitra,
and having placed it in a vessel as prescribed, one should bring it to the temple of Śiva.
In celestial chariots resembling Indra and capable of traveling everywhere,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for ten million times ten thousand divine years.
Having returned here upon the exhaustion of her karma, she shall obtain a beloved husband established with sons and grandsons, and she shall attain enjoyments that are very difficult to acquire.
Having fashioned Mount Kailāsa out of a measure (āḍhaka) of ground rice, adorned with all minerals, and joined with Īśvara and Umā; || 10.153 ||
One should install [the image] in the temple of Īśvara, together with various variegated caves filled with salt-mounds and endowed with all kinds of jewels.
This is called the Kailāsa-vrata; he who performs it on the full moon day of Vaiśākha is honored in the world of Śiva, traveling in vehicles comparable to Mount Kailāsa.
Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in all the worlds beginning with Śiva,
she will eventually come to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
Having fashioned a linga made of flour together with its pedestal in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should worship it with devotion using perfumes and other offerings, and wrap it in a pair of garments.
One should perform a vigil there with various special ornaments;
at dawn, one should offer the banner, conch, and other items to Śiva.
In celestial chariots resembling pure crystal that travel everywhere,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than ten million years.
Having enjoyed all the portions produced from every city according to his desire,
he rejoices in the abode of Śaṅkara with states of being free from worldly play.
Having arrived in this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband;
having fashioned a seven-storied house out of flour in the month of Āṣāḍha.
It was filled with the essence of all seeds and possessed auspicious characteristics;
it was equipped with the implements for the planets, such as pestles, mortars, and so forth.

[The offering] consists of all kinds of jewels, cows, horses, and so forth, adorned with female slaves, beds, and ornaments—all these made of flour (piṣṭamaya), and further graced by lamps and other such items. || 10.163 ||
It was crowded with all kinds of devotees, adorned with perfumes and garlands,
and beautifully decorated with white, red, black, and yellow banners and cloths.
And having installed Śiva before Śivā on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, [one should worship him] with a mirror joined by four feet.
Having prostrated before that which is endowed with all requisites,
one should offer it with great vehicles of a hundred stories— celestial palaces that travel everywhere.
For more than a full hundred million years, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed vast pleasures in all the worlds in succession. (10.167)
Having attained it, one shall obtain a seven-storied mansion enriched with all enjoyments, filled with every kind of mineral wealth, and adorned with various banners. (10.168)
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer a mountain of sesame seeds to Śarva;
[such a person travels] by means of incomparable, auspicious vehicles resembling indranīla gems covered with bark. || 10.169 ||
For more than a full hundred million years, he is honored in the world of Śiva,
having obtained various enjoyments in the various celestial realms.
Having reached this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband,
after having fashioned a beautiful mountain of rice in the month of Bhādrapada.
One should present offerings of canopies, banners, garments, and so forth, as well as relics, [mounted] upon magnificent Great Vehicles that shine like the rays of the sun. (10.172)
For thousands of millions of years, he is honored in the world of Rudra,
having obtained vast enjoyments arising from all the cities.
Having arrived in this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband;
provided that, in the month of Āśvayuja, she has fashioned a vast mountain of grain.
One should offer [this] together with golden garments to Śiva, along with various wonderful great vehicles endowed with excellent enjoyments. (10.175)
For thousands of millions of years he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
having enjoyed desired pleasures in the worlds beginning with the world of Rudra, [he eventually attains liberation].
When this world has arrived [in its proper order], she shall obtain a king as her husband,
endowed with all kinds of grain and all seeds, juices, and so forth.
It is joined with all the elements, adorned with all kinds of jewels, endowed with four peaks, and beautified by canopies and banners. || 10-178 ||
It was adorned with perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps, as well as with various dances and songs, and with conch shells, lutes, and other instruments. (10.179)
It was accompanied by the auspicious sounds of Vedic chants and especially by meritorious benedictions;
it was adorned with eight great banners and made radiant with various beautiful flowers.
One should place the supreme Lord Śiva, surrounded by all the gods, upon the head of the king of serpents named Meru, the highest support of the three worlds.
And by the Daityas, Gandharvas, and Bhūtas, as well as by the hosts of Siddhas and Yakṣas,
by the Vidyādharas, Apsarases, and Nāgas, and especially by the Ṛṣis.
The wise one, having fashioned all the forms out of rice-flour,
should place the trident worshipped by the thirty gods in the right hand of the deity.
In this manner, one should perform the rite with the weapon-mantra for all the deities in their proper sequence,
after having performed the great worship of Śiva accompanied by the prescribed conduct.
One should worship all the gods and offer oblations in the ten directions;
afterwards, one should feed those devoted to Śiva who observe the vow, providing them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should offer to Rudra on the full moon day of Kārttika the most excellent food-offering of rice, prepared with great magnificence and accompanied by every kind of undertaking.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who performs this even once:
whatever merit was previously described by the sages in all the scriptures. (10.187)
One shall obtain that merit multiplied ten millionfold; of this there is no doubt.
[One shall travel] by means of vehicles possessing the luster of great jewels and endowed with all kinds of gems.
Adorned with songs, dances, musical instruments, and beautiful apsarases,
[they travel] in celestial chariots that possess the brilliance of ten million suns and resemble Mount Meru. (10.189)
He was praised by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and the leaders of the gaṇas, amidst auspicious breezes carrying divine fragrances and crowded with men and women.
Having become independent and all-pervading, he proceeds to the excellent abode;
that man of great austerity rejoices there for a hundred divine crores of kalpas.
Thus, having enjoyed all desired pleasures in every world,
she returns here upon the exhaustion of her merit and obtains a king as her husband.
One who is meditated upon as the Lord becomes eternally beautiful and fortunate.
Whatever desire men, women, or eunuchs may have in mind, [it is fulfilled]. (10.193)
One who worships Śiva with devotion shall likewise attain that very state;
[the image] may be fashioned from clay, wood, stone, or brick, provided it is well-prepared. (10.194)
Having constructed a monastery or even a house according to the extent of one's wealth,
provided with all necessary utensils and filled with all kinds of grain.
Having given that house to Śiva, one shall obtain all desires;
provided that, during the winter season, one observes eating only once a day throughout the month of Māgha.
And at the end of the month, one should have a chariot made, adorned with variegated cloths,
yoked to four white oxen, and well-decorated.
Adorned with banners, flowers, and the like, as well as umbrellas, chowries, and mirrors,
one should fashion a linga together with its pedestal out of rice and ground chickpea flour.
Having placed [the image] in the middle of the chariot, one should worship it according to the prescribed characteristics;
then, during that night, [one should carry it] along the royal road with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments. (10.199)
Having whirled [the image] slowly, one should afterwards lead it to the temple of Śiva;
there, it should be adorned with lamps and other offerings, along with vigils and worship. (10.200)
One should gradually pass the night by providing spectacles for viewing;
at dawn, having performed the ritual bath, one should worship (or feed) those who are devoted to him.
One should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability to the wretched, the helpless, and the miserable;
and one should present to Śiva a chariot endowed with beautiful ornamentation.

Having eaten together with his kinsmen and having prostrated before the temple of the Lord, he should perform a sacrifice when this dharma has been completed; for it is the most excellent of all gifts.
The vow named Śivaratha accomplishes all desires and goals;
it possesses the merit found in all vows and the fruit found in all sacrifices.
One shall obtain all that merit in its entirety upon the chariot of Śiva;
[travelling] by means of celestial vehicles that go everywhere and shine like ten thousand suns.
Together with those born of three times seven lineages, he is glorified in the world of Śiva,
having enjoyed vast pleasures in all the worlds in succession.
For more than ten million times ten thousand eons; at the end of that time, he becomes a sovereign lord of the earth, provided with a soft bed adorned with the fivefold cotton coverlet.
One should prepare an auspicious bed equipped with all necessary articles; one should place there an image of Śiva made of flour, joined with an altar.

Having honored with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings an Ācārya who possesses knowledge of the reality of the meaning of Śiva’s wisdom and is endowed with discipline, one should provide him with garments and ornaments. (10.209)
Then, one should offer all kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as a bed;
and whatever the total number of threads in the cotton from which it was made— || 10.210 ||
For that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in all the worlds beginning with Śiva, || 10-211 ||
Having arrived in this world in due course, one shall become a lord of the lion-throne; ten cows with a bull are traditionally known as the "eleven bulls."
Having offered it to Śiva with a purified inner self, he becomes equal in nature to the eleven Rudras through qualities such as power, enjoyment, and the rest. || 10.213 ||
The self-controlled one rejoices at will in all the worlds, beginning with that of Śiva,
for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures together with all those born of his lineage,
he finally attained knowledge through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Being liberated from the turbidity of delusion, one abides in one's very own self;
one should give a hundred cows along with a bull as an exceedingly beautiful offering to Śiva.
Together with those born of his three-times-seven lineages, he shall hear [the teaching] and obtain its fruit;
he shall travel by means of celestial chariots that go everywhere and shine like ten million suns.
Adored by many gods and asuras beyond counting,
he was endowed with the strength of a hundred Rudras, like another Vīrabhadra.
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva, he shall become the sovereign of all;
and after enjoying vast pleasures, at the dissolution of all embodied beings, [he shall attain liberation]. (10.219)
Having cast off the sheath of delusion, one shall attain the knowledge of absolute liberation;
pure and devoted to all sacrifices, one becomes firmly established in one's own self alone.
And being fully perfected, the imperishable Lord of all, like Śiva himself, should give a cow with two faces to Śiva along with exceedingly beautiful [attendants]. (10.221)
One shall obtain that same fruit which is gained by giving the earth with its seven islands, when [the water] has reached as far as the pair of feet and half the head. || 10-222 ||
Then the cow should be known as the Earth as long as she does not release her calf.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Praise of Vows, Fasts, and the Gift of Cows," in the Śivadharmaśāstra.
Glorious One. Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Śrī Nandikeśvara said: For all castes who follow the Śiva-āśrama,
the Śivadharma was taught by Śiva for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a woman, or a Śūdra who has entered the Śiva-order; whether a forest-dweller, a householder, or anyone else who has entered the Śiva-order—11-2.
To the north of his own hermitage, he should establish a very beautiful flower garden;
in the northeast, he should construct a temple for Īśvara, provided with fire and embers.
One should perform [the ritual] at a spot where space is available on the ground;
if possible, one should do so to the south of Śiva, as well as for his devotees. (11.4)
One should worship the Lord at the three junctions of the day and perform the fire-ritual constantly;
or one may worship Śiva with devotion at two junctions or once a day.
One should never eat without having first worshipped Śiva out of delusion;
this is to be known as the supreme dharma, while all other dharmas are said to be secondary.
In cases such as when duties are being neglected, when there is obstruction, or during royal calamities and the like,
one should worship with devotion through the mind, or perform verbal worship by means of recitation and so forth.
Likewise, ascetics residing in the hermitages of Śiva should perform worship;
a yogi should worship with flowers produced in the forest, even if only mentally.
One who harms flowers for the sake of Śiva does not become a perpetrator of violence;
however, if one harms even the slightest thing for one's own sake, then one is indeed a perpetrator of violence. (11-9)

Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva and providing food for his devotees, he should abstain from sexual intercourse on sacred festival days; such a person is a glorious resident of a Śiva-temple hermitage.
One should cook for the sake of the gods, the sacred fire, guests, and mendicants, and never for one's own sake alone.
He who, out of delusion, cooks for his own sake, lives only for the purpose of hell.
For those whose cooking is for the sake of the gods, whose sexual union is for the sake of progeny,
and whose life is for the sake of heaven— for them, the opposite leads to hell.
One should perform the worship of Śiva with one-third of one's wealth,
or even with half of that, for life is indeed transient.
One should acquire wealth through righteous means and avoid that which is unrighteous;
for he who lives by wealth acquired through unrighteous means lives only for the sake of hell. (11.14)
He who is auspicious and a celibate student, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva and the sacred fire,
should be one who has conquered his senses, peaceful, whether he be a lifelong student or one observing a specific vow.
Completely liberated from all attachments, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits,
one should know Śiva through the mind and become devoted to the worship of Śiva and the sacred fire.

Withdrawn from all attachments and devoted to the meditation on Śiva, he who is established in the sacred ash and has conquered his senses should be known as one for whom Śiva is the very emblem. || 11.17 ||

One should wear bracelets of rudrākṣa on the hand, as well as around the neck and on the head; likewise, those established in the stage of Śiva (śivāśrama) should bear the liṅga and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with sacred ash.
Whoever wears a rudrākṣa on the hand, on the head, or on the chest,
becomes unapproachable by all beings and goes to the world of Rudra. (11.19)
This [liṅga] should always be worn by the devotees of Rudra as equal to Rudra himself;
he whose sole occupation is a flower garden, engaged in the activities of a flower grove. (11-20)
Constantly engaged in the worship of the three ablutions and clad only in a loincloth, one attains the station of Yoga through the yoga of devotion to the yogis. || 11-21 ||

Those devoted to the meditation on Śiva, those who are tranquil, and those dedicated to the dharma of Śiva—all stages of life (āśramas) should be known as devotees of Śiva who take refuge in Śiva. || 11-22 ||
The eight great vows (mahāvratāṣṭaka) declared by the Lord should be observed by those seeking Śiva;
this is the supreme among all vows, in which dharma is fully perfected. (11.23)
Devotion to Śiva, constant forbearance, non-violence, perpetual compassion, contentment, truthfulness, non-stealing, and likewise celibacy—this is the group of eight. (11–124)
One should always cultivate devotion toward Śiva through worship as far as possible by means of action, mind, and speech; and likewise toward the yogis of Śiva. (11.25)
One should protect devotees of Śiva no differently than one's own body, and one should do what is pleasing for them, shielding them from fear, poverty, and disease. (11.26)
What indeed can be done by people for Śiva, who is already perfectly complete?
Whatever is performed for the devotees of Śiva is always performed for Śiva himself. (11.27)
One must travel even a very great distance to where there is a person devoted to Maheśvara;
for Hara is present there, and he should be sought with diligent effort.
A devotee of Maheśvara who is devoted to the worship of Śiva shall,
by performing worship according to the prescribed rule, obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice. || 11-29 ||
Constantly devoted to the stories of Śiva and always intent upon Śiva,
a man who worships according to the prescribed rule shall attain the status of the Lord of Ganas.
One should devoutly honor a devotee of Śiva who has come to his hermitage with a welcome, a seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, madhuparka, and other foods. (11.31)
He who offers a greeting or even a salutation upon [the Buddha's] arrival is honored in the world of Agni for ten thousand years. (11.32)
He who personally offers a seat to one who has arrived as a devotee of Śiva shall dwell in the city of Purandara for twenty thousand years.
Having diligently washed the feet of a Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva, one should anoint them with ghee with devotion; such a person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
By the gift of a shelter, one shall have a golden house in heaven;
by giving very cool water, one shall obtain all desires.
By the gift of a lamp, one obtains the eye of knowledge that transcends the senses;
by the gift of a soft bed, one becomes a lord upon a lion-throne.
Having likewise performed a bath with water, which increases good fortune and luster,
one who performs the ritual bath according to the rules shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
One who fans with a palm-leaf fan a person whose limbs are covered in beads of sweat and who is radiant from the exhaustion of a journey shall attain the world of Vāyu.
By protecting one who is afflicted by hunger and thirst, one who is peaceful yet distressed, or one who is impure and diseased, to the best of one's ability, one is liberated from all sins. (11.39)
Having diligently brought about the welfare of one afflicted by disease through medicines and other means,
one is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of yugas.
He who especially protects a devotee of Śiva afflicted by disease, through medicines and the granting of a livelihood, will certainly go to the world of Śiva. || 11-41 ||
If one should restore someone to health with great effort, he shall become a member of Śiva’s family; his merit is infinite. (11.42)
Returning here from that time, having reached the further shore of all knowledge,
he shall attain the state of Rudra, which is the destruction of all sufferings.
He who applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with white ashes at the three junctions of the day is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 11.44 ||
That which is the supreme potency of the fire of Rudra is proclaimed as ash;
it destroys all sufferings and purifies all sins. (11.45)
The yogi should daily perform a full-body bath from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head at the three junctions of the day; he shall quickly attain yoga. (11.46)
One who, with senses restrained, constantly performs the fire-sacrifice (āgneya-yajña) shall deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage and attain the supreme state.
The cow-dung produced from cows of pure lineage by their own nature,
when further cooked by the fire of Śiva, is remembered as the sacred ash (bhasma).
The ash-bath possesses innumerable qualities superior to the water-bath;
therefore, having abandoned the Varuṇa bath, one should perform the Āgneya bath. (11.49)
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices—one obtains all that fruit from the ash-bath; of this there is no doubt.
One who is joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) and joined with all sins should practice the ash-bath; thus one is released from all sins. || 11-51 ||
There is no purifying bath superior to the ash-bath;
this was declared to all the gods by Śiva himself, who bathed therein. (11.52)
From that time forward, Brahmā and the others, as well as the sages seeking Śiva’s favor,
diligently performed the ash-bath on all sacred festival days.
Therefore, he who performs this Agneya bath of Śiva shall undoubtedly become Rudra himself in this very body; of this there is no doubt. (11.54)
Whether one is immoral or endowed with virtue, or whether one possesses no auspicious marks at all,
such a person is worthy of worship due to their union with the Lord, just like a prince.
Because one who honors the food offered to a virtuous recipient becomes a worshiper of the Teaching, one should therefore worship the Teaching without hesitation, by the command of Śiva. (11.56)
That which is the supreme virility of the fire of Rudra is proclaimed as ash;
because it is the burner of all sufferings, it is therefore called "bhasma. (11.57)
By worshipping the fire of Śiva, Śiva himself is directly worshipped;
therefore, one whose mind is free from conceptual construction should worship the teaching of Śiva. (11.58)
For even he who, though through deceit, maintains a course according to the Lord’s teaching, attains a destination that cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices. (11.59)
According to the rite of sipping water (ācamana), one should always touch water with pure Śiva-ash for the purpose of purifying any lingering scent or stain. (11.60)
Even if free from the taint of perfumes and ointments, one whose internal disposition is impure is not purified,
even by thousands of water-jars or hundreds of loads of clay.
Even in a thousand years, one whose inner disposition is impure does not become pure;
one should practice purification purified by the disposition, and drink water filtered through a cloth. (11.62)
One should set down one's foot purified by vision; one should speak words purified by truth.
Even if one possesses a mass of matted hair, one should perform a shave at the end of each fortnight.
Whatever merit is found in the initiation ceremony, that same merit is obtained when the shaving of the head has been performed.
Whether one has matted hair, a shaven head, or a top-knot, one should subsist on alms, free from all longing. (11.64)
A silent ascetic, compassionate toward all beings and tranquil in mind, should wander about; performing virtuous deeds, he should subsist on alms-food and avoid eating food from a single source.
Alms-food is superior to fasting; for a householder, eating at a single person's place is a stain.
He who is liberated from all attachments, pure, and devoted solely to Śiva— [is truly free]. (11.66)
Having performed the tonsure here as well, he shall become an attendant of the Lord of Yogins;
righteous in his devotion to Śiva, he shall dwell eternally in the sanctuary together with his retinue.
Having consoled one who has come for refuge, who is distressed, and who is beset by enemies and thieves,
saying "Do not fear," he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having rescued, to the best of one's ability, that great being who is unconscious and submerged in the ocean of poverty, one shall obtain all desires. (11.69)
When food has fallen, or when it is mixed with the remains of a corpse, a Caṇḍāla, or birds, one should give that food to all living beings according to one's ability out of compassion. (11.170)
Even a very small gift, when given out of compassion, becomes inexhaustible;
therefore, among all beings, giving out of compassion is supreme.
In the absence [of other things], by giving grass, ground, water, leaves, roots, or fruits out of compassion to one who has arrived, or even with affection, they go to heaven. (11.72)
Such is this staircase to heaven as those who speak kindly are in this world;
for them, there is happiness both here and hereafter, and their voices are sweet when they speak.
Having spoken words that flow with nectar, cool as the touch of sandalwood,
and not contrary to the Dharma, one shall attain imperishable happiness.
O best of Brahmins, neither by the giving of land, nor by officiating at sacrifices, nor by Vedic study,
is there such a stainless staircase to heaven as these words which are so dear.
Rising to meet [others], approaching them, acting with compliance, pleasant speech, being the first to speak, and showing hospitality—each of these is a cause for heaven. (11.76)
One should affectionately inquire after the visitor's well-being and likewise offer water for refreshment;
when he departs, one should likewise say: "May your paths be auspicious. (11.77)
May there be constant auspiciousness for you for the sake of accomplishing all goals; may this blessing of speech always attend you in all undertakings. (11.78)
In salutations and greetings, one should utter words expressive of well-being and auspiciousness; in all ritual actions, one should say, "May there be prosperity everywhere. (11.79)
Having thus practiced such Śiva-conduct, the inhabitant of the Śiva-order,
liberated from all sins without exception, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The devotion that is performed by men who are devotees of those [other] devotees of Śiva becomes devotion toward Śiva itself; such devotion is practiced by those devoted to devotion. (11.81)
Whether reviled or even beaten, he who does not revile in turn nor strike back—neither by word nor by deed, remaining composed—it is patience alone that is prescribed for him. (11.82)
He is a hero, one of sattvic nature, a wise man, an ascetic, and one who has conquered his senses—he by whom the enemy's wrath was utterly defeated with the weapon of patience. (11.83)
Forgiveness is the gift, forgiveness is truth, forgiveness is non-violence, and forgiveness is sacred learning;
forgiveness is both heaven and liberation—for by forgiveness alone is the world sustained. (11.84)
Among all sacred fords, the one who has reached the further shore of knowledge is the true ford;
those who have bathed in the waters of knowledge possess a sacred ford superior to any other.
Knowledge, yoga, austerity, recitation, and virtuous deeds such as sacrifice and charity—all these are in vain for one who is prone to anger; therefore, one should abandon anger.
Unpleasant speech may burn the vital points, the bones, the life-force, and the heart; therefore, one should not speak what is unpleasant, especially toward a devotee of Śiva. (11.87)
Having completed [the practice] with the stainless waters of patience, which are as cool as wealth,
one attains happiness in this world and a blissful state in the next.
He who constantly acts for the welfare and the auspiciousness of all beings as he does for himself— this is declared to be non-violence (ahiṃsā). (11.89)
Whatever fruit is obtained through all the scriptures, the Vedas, and sacrifices, the merit of those who do not harm living beings is even greater than that. (11.90)
Even if one were to give away the entire three worlds filled with jewels,
or perform all forms of austerity, these would not equal non-violence.
This non-violence is proclaimed as the supreme duty for those who are capable;
for those who are incapable, this duty consists primarily of charity, sacrifice, and the like.
We do not perceive anything superior to this anywhere in any scripture;
indeed, the gift that bestows fearlessness upon men is a wondrous and supreme gift.
Having granted fearlessness to all beings, he who moves about with a tranquil mind finds no fear from any beings even in this very world.
He who does not harm living beings, whether stationary or moving, enjoys supreme and unsurpassed peace, free from suffering. (11.95)
For the wicked, cruel, and lowest of men take delight in evil deeds;
they are cooked in the fires of hell until the dissolution of all beings.
The king who shall effect the prevention of the slaughter of living beings in his own country rejoices for a long time in prosperity, together with that kingdom. (11.97)
And at the end of the body, together with his entire family, he is honored in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions of kalpas, enjoying great pleasures.
But he who, whether for his own sake or for the sake of others, restrains all his senses and does not engage in what should not be done— him they call one characterized by tranquility. (11.99)
He whose collection of senses is thoroughly pacified and who is as pure as the rays of the moon,
attains the supreme state of Śiva with a tranquil mind.
Contentment is proclaimed as that state of being satisfied with whatever has been obtained, whatever has arisen, and whatever wealth has been acquired through righteous means. (11.101)
While living amidst present objects, past and future, one does not recollect those things that have passed; this is what is called contentment. (11.102)
By him everything has been rendered free from enmity; by him austerity has been attained and performed.
By him, having abandoned the state of craving, contentment has been properly embraced. (11.103)
The happiness that belongs to those of peaceful mind who possess the sovereignty of contentment—that same happiness is experienced by gods, asuras, and humans even in heaven. (11.104)
To not conceal what one has personally experienced or seen—that is, the facts as they were perceived—and to speak of matters exactly as they are: this is the definition of truth. (11.105)
Furthermore, this truth is indeed truth; it is the characteristic of both truth and untruth.
As long as speech is free from harming others, it shall be auspicious.
That truth is superior to the horse sacrifice by many qualities;
knowledge is established in truth, and dharma is established in truth.
Purity is established in truth, and liberation is established in truth; [this applies] to those protected by their master and to those abandoned during times of distress. (11.108)

This non-appropriation of the property of others is the defining characteristic of non-stealing; it is that which does not engage, even in the slightest degree, with the property of others when they do not give it. (11.109)
Through action, mind, and speech, being thus satisfied, one shall attain the state of Śiva;
this consists of refraining from sexual conduct and not speaking of it there with the mind.
The defining characteristic of the holy life is the restraint of all the sense faculties;
purity is established in the holy life, and austerity is established in the holy life.
Knowledge is established in celibacy; forbearance is established in celibacy.
Those who abide by celibacy are eternally established in Śiva.
The destiny attained by a celibate student who has stayed for even a single night cannot be reached by those seized by the planets, even through hundreds of sacrifices.
Having abandoned all attachments, he remains with a mind undisturbed;
oh, this illustrious and best of ascetics does not lose his mindfulness even at the moment of death.
He who, having abandoned women and avoided other wives,
remains united [with his own] and is a celibate student (brahmacārī) and equanimous, should be known as such in the Śiva-āgama.
One should perform all actions for the sake of Śiva, the sacred fire, guests, and teachers;
such a person should be known as non-violent, and he attains the state of Rudra upon this earth.
A person who is always diligently engaged in the service of Śiva, the sacred fire, and the guru—his undertakings succeed, even those merely conceived in his mind. (11.117)
This glorious tree of Dharma, originating from Śiva, has eight branches;
it cannot be described in detail due to the proliferation of its sub-branches.
Those who recite with devotion this supreme meditation on one's own teacher before Śiva,
are glorified in the world of Śiva together with those born of twenty-one generations of their lineage. (11.119)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Conduct of Śiva’s Stages of Life," in the Śivadharmaśāstra proclaimed by Nandikeśvara.
p. 141(167) Śrī. Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Nandikeśvara said: Now, out of compassion for those who have become devoted to Śiva, I shall briefly explain the meaning of the primary branches and sub-branches, which arise from devotion to Śiva.
Whenever, while traveling somewhere, one sees a Śiva-liṅga that has not been worshipped, one should worship it and then proceed; there is no doubt that one goes accompanied by Rudra.

One should not accept baths, food offerings, clothing, and other such pleasant things; for that which has been renounced in honor of Śiva becomes fruitless through [subsequent] giving. (The fruit thereof is lost. 12-3.

Having seen a sacred site (āyatana), one should depart from it after paying homage; likewise, upon seeing a crossroads, a river, a mountain, or a yogin of Śiva, one should proceed toward Śiva after offering salutation.
Having descended, saluted, and beheld the Linga, the one of firm vows [alighted] from his elephant,
vehicle, seat, and horse before the ascetic who was a Śiva-yogin.
Even while staying there, having offered salutations, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
[One should avoid] the flesh of deer, horses, camels, and poultry, as well as garlic and *grañjana*.
One should always strictly avoid the power derived from mercury and other such substances,
as well as the merit of all gifts, fierce austerities, and the Ashvamedha sacrifice.
One attains the fruit without effort simply by abstaining from liquor and meat;
since liquor is the locus of all defects, one should avoid it from afar. (12.8)

Where is liquor, and where is devotion to Śiva? Where is meat, and where is the worship of Śiva? Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords (tīrthas), and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices— || 12-9 ||
He who completely abstains from intoxicants obtains all that fruit [of the rites],
whether it be the various consecratory ceremonies beginning with conception or the funeral feast at the end in the cremation ground.
A devotee of Śiva should avoid anything touched by a woman in her menses or similar persons;
he should not step over a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, ashes, fire, a Liṅga, or a shadow.
One should not step over the remains of offerings (nirmālya); one should place them in water or on the ground.
One should wear the nirmālya of Śiva with devotion, but one should not wear it out of greed.
By eating [the forbidden food], one goes to hell, as does that fool who transgresses it;
Śaṅkara does not accept bathing, worship, or other offerings there.
Just as one might [view] a certain region of the earth adorned with one's own body. || 12-14 ||
He too would become untouchable, just like one who has touched the filth of his own limbs;
therefore, a man defiled by the remains of offerings (nirmālya) must not touch the liṅga.
But Śaṅkara does not accept that bath which is performed merely out of devotion.
One should avoid disparaging the eight forms of Śiva, as well as the guru, devotees of Śiva, kings, virtuous people, and ascetics. (12–17)
On the eighth and other such days, as well as on the fifth day of both fortnights,
one should avoid shaving, the application of collyrium, anointing with oil, sexual intercourse, and similar activities.
One should perform worship especially at this time and observe the practice of eating only at night;
one should also perform purification with earth and water to remove the clinging of perfumes and ointments. (12.19)
He who should eat food without having bathed would consume nothing but sin;
therefore, one should eat after bathing with either ashes or water.
Having bathed in the morning with water, one should go to the auspicious state through the ash-bath;
having cast off the garment of sin, one should offer seven sesame seeds.
One should perform the commencement of the great worship every four months;
food should be provided, and one should arrange for offerings according to one's capacity.
Accompanied by his three-times-seven lineages and surrounded by all his attendants, he shall dwell eternally in the city of Śiva due to the performance of the Cāturmāsya rite.
Thus, during every festival, at a śrāddha ceremony, and on auspicious days,
having worshipped Śiva with food offerings, one should feed the Śiva-yogins.
The ancestors and all the gods abide by taking refuge in Śiva;
when Śiva is pleased, they all become well-pleased—of this there is no doubt.
In śrāddha rites, one should feed a Śiva-yogin who is endowed with knowledge and dispassion, devoted to the sacred ash, has conquered his senses, and possesses a tranquil mind.

If, through the discernment of thorough knowledge regarding principles such as Īśvara and so forth, there arises similarity and dissimilarity, this is the defining characteristic of that knowledge. (12.27)
The attainment of what is desired does not last, nor does one rejoice in what is desired;
through the distress of loss and the despair of failure, one transcends worldly attachment.
The fruit that is obtained in even a single day by one who is established in the final stage of the ash-observance cannot be attained by a householder, even through hundreds of sacrifices. (12.29)
With his senses subdued and his self serene, he neither hates nor desires;
one who does not crave the enjoyments of sense-objects such as sound and the rest should be known as a master of his senses.
Endowed with knowledge and dispassion, possessing a peaceful mind, and disciplined in the yoga of six limbs—he is proclaimed a Śivayogin. (12.31)
From the Śiva-dharma arises knowledge; from knowledge arises the birth of dispassion (vairāgya).
For one endowed with both knowledge and dispassion, Śiva-yoga proceeds. (12.32)
Through the yoga of Śiva, one becomes omniscient and eternally perfect;
established in one's own self and pure, one becomes all-pervading like Śiva. ||33||
The Puruṣa is remembered as the highest of all beings;
among Puruṣas, the twice-born is superior; and among the twice-born, one who has mastered the Vedas is the best.
The knower of the meaning of reality excels over those who know the Vedas through their knowledge of fragrances;
and the awakened one excels over those who know the various categories of the principles of reality. (12.35)
Yogis who know the various principles are considered superior;
and the supreme Śiva and Śivā are superior to hundreds of millions of such yogis.

The ancestors who possess yoga-knowledge, who have attained perfection in yoga, and who are born of yoga, are especially gratified by those who have consumed [the offerings] belonging to Śiva-yogins. || 12-37 ||
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and meritorious deeds performed,
one obtains all that fruit by fully honoring a Śiva-yogin.
The sacrificial animal, the fire, Rudra, Time as the self, and likewise the southern offering-fire—
through their conjunction with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, this is proclaimed as the Vedic sacrifice. (12.39)
Celibacy, recitation, silence, forbearance, and moderation in food—
such is the formidable form of austerity, characterized by these five features.
Whatever is desirable, excellent, and obtained through righteous means—that gift given to one possessed of virtues is the defining characteristic of giving. (12.41)
To give land endowed with water, measuring a thousand nivartanas and capable of producing all kinds of crops— that is called the gift of land.
Whatever king, having brought the earth under a single umbrella, should bestow it upon the twice-born in its entirety, that is called the "gift of the earth. (12.43)

One should give a well-adorned maiden, endowed with virtuous qualities, to a twice-born man who is a performer of sacrifices and possessed of Vedic knowledge; that is called the gift of a maiden (kanyādāna).
Having given a well-adorned maiden—free from all defects, youthful, and possessing excellent qualities—to a Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva, [one attains the aforementioned reward]. (12.45)
He who gives a cow adorned [with ornaments], that is declared to be the gift of a cow (godāna).
Furthermore, he who gives new garments of middling or superior quality— || 12-46 ||
This, in brief, should be known as the characteristic of the gift of clothing:
one who is a celibate student, established in meditative concentration, patient, and devoted to moral discipline. (12.47)
One should not eat for a day and night; this is the characteristic of the fast:
namely, two hundred and forty morsels of food.

Restraining [the senses] and eating according to one's desire is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow by the sages who are learned in all scriptures, devoted to austerity, and have conquered their senses. (12.49)
A sacred ford (tīrtha) on earth that is frequented by the gods is called a tīrtha;
one should point out the holy fields (puṇyakṣetra) as the locations where the incarnations of Rudra reside.
For embodied beings who die within those auspicious fields (śivakṣetra), there is the state of Rudra;
likewise for those who establish groves, dwellings, wells, gardens, or places for the libation of the gods. || 12-51 ||
Whoever performs these [rites] at sacred fords (tīrthas) obtains imperishable fruit:
forgiveness, freedom from desire, compassion, truthfulness, generosity, good conduct, and likewise learning. (12.52)
This is declared to be the supreme eightfold characteristic of a worthy recipient;
[it includes] the fruits of sacrifice, fasting, giving, austerity, and pilgrimage.
Having worshipped with devotion and according to one's means, one obtains a Śiva-yogin—
one who is a devotee of Śiva, patient, truthful, and possesses complete restraint over all the senses.
Loving-kindness toward all beings is the characteristic of the Śiva-dharma;
he who is a practitioner of Śiva-yoga, a knower of Śiva-knowledge, and devoted to the Śiva-dharma [is such a one]. (12.55)
Thus, these three types are to be known as the characteristics of the vessel of Śiva:
that which is given for the sake of Śiva, without regard for the recipient's qualities or status. (12.56)
Wealth given to those devoted to the Lord is the characteristic of a gift to Śiva;
he who feeds an excellent Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva at śrāddha ceremonies and other rites [attains great merit]. (12.57)
Having uplifted seven generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
What more need be said here? One should feed a devotee of Śiva. (12.58)
When a devotee of Śiva eats, Sadāśiva himself eats directly.
Whatever fruit is obtained by honoring ten million twice-born ones who are learned in the Vedas— [that fruit is attained by the devotee of Śiva]. (12.59)
The fruit of giving alms to a sage who is free from passion is great;
therefore, one should especially give at a śrāddha ceremony and on auspicious days. (12.60)
One should feed a preeminent brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva, with Śiva in mind, whether he be unrestrained or self-controlled, even if he has fallen into any state whatsoever. (12.61)
Whosoever is a devotee of Śiva is the most excellent vessel, equal to Śiva himself;
even one who worships Rudra out of association or greed for wealth [is likewise worthy]. (12.62)
Even by means of hundreds of sacrifices, one does not attain that destination which he attains;
therefore, he is always to be honored, worshiped, and protected.
But he who has taken refuge in the Name alone, even for half a moment in Śiva—he is a sage, a great saint, and a yogi; he shall attain the state of Śiva.

The merit that is obtained from a śrāddha performed during a planetary transit is increased a hundredfold when done in a forest; it should be known as ten-thousandfold by a river, and infinite at the abode of Śiva.
Whoever offers with devotion a soft seat made of vetra grass shall obtain that merit which is ten thousand times greater than the merit found in the hermitages of Śiva.
Or one may become a lord upon a lion-throne made of ivory;
by offering a garment for covering the loins to a Śiva-yogin, [one attains this]. (12.67)
Having given a broad woolen cloak to a Śiva-yogin, one is glorified in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions of yugas.
One shall obtain the fruit of having given gold for every single hair [of the hide].
The skins of deer, leopards, and other such animals, when rubbed with sesame paste, [yield this merit]. (12.69)
Having offered soft, dyed-red garments to a Śiva-yogin, [one obtains the merit of] as many skins of deer, leopards, and so forth as there are hairs upon them. (12.70)
He who provides purifying offerings of water and land to a Śiva-yogin is honored in the world of Rudra for as many hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
And by providing protection for all living beings, one shall dwell in heaven for a hundred thousand years; so too for one who gives a water-pot equipped with a triple-strand rope.
Having given great lakes, one obtains all that merit;
[one should take] very fine clay, free from the defects of living beings. (12.73)
By offering these to the Śiva-yogins, one obtains the fruit of gifting land;
likewise, by offering vessels made of clay, ashes, bamboo, or gourd. (12.74)
By offering [these] to the Śiva-yogins, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
likewise, by offering a handful of tooth-sticks to a Śiva-yogin, one gains the same merit.
By offering sacred yoga-bands and purificatory items to a Śiva-yogin, one shall obtain a divine and beautiful city endowed with the enjoyments of celestial women.
One shall obtain the fruit of having given a thousand pairs of garments,
as well as an alms-bowl made of clay, along with its stand and other vessels.
By offering [these] to the Śiva-yogins, one shall always obtain the fruit of a perpetual sacrifice;
likewise, he who gives sandals or wooden shoes to a devotee of Śiva [attains the same].
One who gives a spotted staff, or another [staff], to a Śiva-yogin would obtain the fruit of giving a thousand bay horses. (12.79) p. 149(175)
One whose soul is endowed with the support of strength may become a leader at the head of the army;
or, he who would give a palm-leaf fan or a parasol to a Śiva-yogin [attains the same]. (12.80)
That lord of men would rule the earth under a single umbrella, especially when it comes to the remnants in the bowls of the Śiva-yogins. (12.81)
He who gives this great book to one devoted to the knowledge of Śiva shall become a glorious lord of the earth, the support of his lineage, and endowed with noble descent. (12.82)
He is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred times ten million divine yugas;
having returned here, he becomes illustrious, wealthy, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
He who speaks for the sake of all-knowledge, equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect, who is a yogi of Śiva, a knower of Śiva’s wisdom, and one devoted to the dharma of Śiva—[to him one should give]. (12.84)
Having worshipped Śiva, one who is equal-minded and remembered as possessing qualities equal to all—whether he himself builds or causes to be built a temple for a Śiva-yogin—is so described. (12.85)
For a hundred thousand years, one is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments;
that Rudra becomes [one's own self] through the gift of rudrākṣas—what wonder is there in this? (12.86)
By means of that garland, Rudra is always transferred into the hand on this earth;
for the rudrākṣas are themselves Rudras, as are those who wear rudrākṣas.
Therefore, one should wear rudrākṣas here, for Rudra is within them and beyond them.
He who always wears a rudrākṣa rosary around his neck or in the palm of his hand— || 12-88 ||
By means of half of half of one hundred [beads], he becomes Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
For even animals, when joined with rudrākṣa beads, attain the state of Rudra. (12.89)
How much more so for a man who here moves a rosary of rudrākṣa beads?
Whatever mantra he recites while moving the garland in this manner, that shall indeed be accomplished; of this there is no doubt. (12.90)
And the recitation of Rudra-mantras [yields] merit a hundred million times greater than that,
provided one has placed a rosary of rudrākṣa beads upon the head or on the sacred thread.
And whoever eats while his body is smeared with ashes has, without a doubt, eaten the food of the Rudras;
therefore, the wearing of rudrākṣa beads is always highly praised.
For the sake of favoring the welfare of others, especially that of a Brahmin, one should give whatever implements are necessary, even if they are few, according to one's ability. (12.93)
For a hundred thousand years, he is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments;
furthermore, he should construct a well-guarded dwelling for the Śiva-yogins.
One obtains as much fruit of merit as is contained within the temple of Śiva that has been built;
for as is Śiva, so is the yogi, and as is the yogi, so is Śiva. (12.95)
Therefore, one should offer even a small amount of alms, such as a hundred thousand [gold pieces], at the feet of the lords of yogis;
whatever may be of use to him should be given to him with great effort.
By both providing instruction and making offerings, one gains merit from both;
having constructed an excellent pavilion for the exposition of the Śivadharma.
One should place there the seat for the Guru, adorned with cloths, flowers, and other ornaments;
the auspicious seat of Śivadharma, likewise adorned with cloths, flowers, and so forth. (12.98)
Having placed [the manuscript] before that teacher, one should then worship both the teacher who proclaims the Śiva-dharma and the reciter. (12.99)
One should worship the Śivadharma as well, for these three are equal; for he who explains the Śivadharma and the word "Śiva" according to the proper method [is worthy of honor]. (12.100)
Having obtained long life, knowledge, fame, and happiness, he shall go to Śiva at the end;
thus has this eternal Śivadharma been fully described to you. (12.101)
This should be told by one who possesses knowledge to all devotees of Śiva:
"The devotee who proclaims the Śiva-dharma in the hermitages of Śiva... (12.102).
Or one who hears it—by those two, the entire fruit mentioned here shall be obtained. Having thus heard the entirety of dharma as proclaimed by the son of Brahmā, [one attains the goal]. (12.103)
And it was said that the twelve-chapter treatise on Dharma, whose essence is Śiva, was taught to Candra Ātreya, who belonged to the same lineage and was a devotee of Śiva. (12.104)
As long as one practices the Śiva-dharma through his instruction, so long does he also obtain that merit from the instruction; of this there is no doubt. (12.105)
Since dharma cannot be known without instruction, nor can it be practiced without being known, the fruit for both is equal. (12.106)
The instructor, the consenter, the doer, the one who causes to do, and the protector of what has been done—these five are declared to have equal shares in the fruit. (12.107)
One who maintains what has been established by another gains even greater merit than the original builder;
for a sanctuary quickly goes to ruin through lack of maintenance.
For lands, jewels, horses, elephants, cattle, gold, and so forth, as well as garments—
regarding those previously mentioned— it is better to protect what one already possesses than to give them away. (12.109)
The merit of one who protects what has been given is even greater than that of the giver;
for that which is not protected perishes very quickly.
Therefore, one should teach the Dharma, practice it oneself as well, cause others to perform it, approve of what has been done by others, and protect it. (12.111)
Thus, this fivefold Śiva-dharma has been proclaimed:
Rudrapāda, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, and Mahālaya. (12.112)
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Suvarṇākṣa, and the radiant Adīptimān, as well as Sthāṇvīśvara, which is renowned and celebrated throughout the three worlds. (12.113)
This group of eight sites should be known as the highly auspicious Rudrakṣetra;
beginning with Vastrāpada and ending with Sthāṇu, it is the cause for attaining union (sāyujya) with Rudra.
Jalagaṇḍa, Upiraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kālañjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthala, and the supreme Sthūleśvara. (12.115)
This [section] called the Pavitrāṣṭaka increases great merit;
those who die there go directly to the supreme abode of Śiva.
Gaya, Kurukṣetra, Nakhala, and likewise Kanaka;
Vimaleśvara, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīma—these are the eight.
This is known as the "Eightfold Secret," which purifies all sins;
a man who dies [while reciting it] attains the glorious abode of Śiva.
Śrīparvata, Hariścandra, Jalpa, Ābhrādikeśvara, Madhyama, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava. (12.119)
This most secret of secrets is proclaimed as the eightfold [rite].
When all the ancestors are satisfied by it, they go to Śiva, the supreme state. (12.120)
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara;
Āṣāḍha, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍa, Bhārabhūmi, and Bhavāntika.
And the famous Lagulīśa, as well as the great Pratyātmaka;
this field of Rudra, consisting of eight such sites, grants all desires.
There, all who have died go to the supreme abode of Rudra;
this should be known as the "Eightfold Merit," which is the cause for attaining union with Śiva.

Whoever performs a Śrāddha, a sacrifice, austerity, or the recitation of mantras, as well as bathing, giving gifts, or observing vows at these sacred fords (tīrthas), shall obtain inexhaustible fruit for that deed.
Forgiveness, longing [for the good], compassion, truthfulness, generosity, moral conduct, austerity, and learning—
this is declared to be the eightfold supreme characteristic of a worthy recipient.

For the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and out of compassion for all beings, one is the doer, the one who causes others to act, the end-maker, the instigator, and the one who rejoices in the deed. (12.126)
Thus, this fivefold Śivadharma has been proclaimed.
O Lord of Devas, garlanded with skulls, Mahākāla, homage be to you! (12.127)
O Lord of Gaurī, whose head is the crescent moon, who holds a shield, noose, and sword in your hands;
O Master who wears an elephant hide, O Caṇḍanātha, homage be to you!
O Lord of gods, wielder of the trident, three-eyed one, sovereign of the thirty [gods],
O Mahādeva of triple form, destroyer of Tripura— homage be to you! (12.129)
Lord of all, omnipresent, all-knowing, with faces on every side, abiding everywhere—you are all; may you, the Pervader, be victorious! (12.130)

Salutations to You, by whom the moving and the unmoving are pervaded through the distinction of gross and subtle; O You who are infinite, beginningless, perfectly manifest, both manifest and unmanifest!
I bow to the infinite, eternal, universal, auspicious, and perpetual Lord of Umā;
to Śrīkaṇṭha, to Sarpakaṇṭha, and to Nīlakaṇṭha. (12–132)
I bow to Him whose body is composed of the Brahman, who abides beyond all knowledge,
who is both with parts and without parts, and who is devoid of time.
Lord of yoga, composed of yoga, whose self is yoga, born of yoga;
O Lord of Yoga, you who are devoted to the great yoga, salutations again and again!
O you who consist of all splendor, the splendor even of splendors, the teacher of splendors, the embodiment of splendor, O radiant one, beyond all splendor— salutations be to you!
By the single syllable "Om," you have been explained throughout the three worlds;
O Sadāśiva, salutations to you, who are eternally devoted to its true meaning.
O you who are half a mātrā, the supreme limit, even half of that, the beyond-the-supreme, the supreme, the beyond-the-supreme, the peaceful, and that which transcends peace— salutations to you!
Above the vowels *a* and *u*, that which is the syllable *ma*, the very *bindu*—O you who are beyond *nirvāṇa*, beyond the supreme, and beyond all principles (*tattva*), homage be to you! (12-138)
O Śiva, O Peaceful One, homage be to you, whose splendor is but a hundredth part of a hundredth of the morning sun, and who possess an incomparable celestial palace. 12-139.
I bow to that which is infinite, beginningless, unmanifest, residing within the body yet devoid of a body,
situated in the hearts of all beings, and pervading the sky.
Incomprehensible even by the senses, devoid of all objective entities,
the Self is concealed by its own splendor— the supreme beyond the great illusion (mahāmāyā).
I bow to that which transcends the supreme great knowledge, which is accessible through wisdom,
the single syllable with its four divisions, adorned with the four measures.
I bow to the four-fold, that which transcends the parts (kalās), and that which transcends the seed-syllables (bījas).
O Īśāna, O Īśvara, O Brahmā, O Sadāśiva, homage be to you!
For the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and out of compassion for all living beings,
the Śiva-dharma was proclaimed by Nandin to Āsanaka and others.
The speaker, the listener, and the one who approves of this shall be glorified in the world of Śiva.
May all be happy; may all be free from disease. (12.145)
May all behold auspicious things and may they transcend all sufferings;
at the end of their bodies, may all people attain liberation and go to the state of Śiva.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śivadharmottara, a Śaiva scripture proclaimed by Nandikeśvara.
May there be auspiciousness! Om! The Śivadharmottara is completed. Salutations to Dakṣiṇāmūrti!
Oṃ.
